News.title: Summer 2026 on course to be UK's hottest on record, says Met Office
News.content:
This summer is on course to be the UK's hottest since records began, according to the Met Office.

Only average conditions are needed for the remainder of August to surpass the record set just last year.

Provisional Met Office statistics show that the UK's mean temperature for meteorological summer so far (1 June to 10 August) currently stands at 16.48C, which is 1.88C above the 1991-2020 average.

In summer 2025, the mean temperature across the country - which includes overnight lows as well as daytime highs - was 16.10C (60.98F).

It is in line with evidence that summers are getting hotter and drier because of climate change.

News.title: Eclipse chasers scramble for glasses as stocks run low
News.content:
At a bakery in central London, stock has been flying off the shelves.

"I've sold, like, 100 this morning," a staff member tells the BBC. But it's not baked goods driving queues out of the door - customers are here to buy eclipse glasses.

They are among those hoping to catch a safe glimpse of Wednesday's solar eclipse - the UK's most significant since 1999 - but struggling to get their hands on the right gear.

Experts have urged eclipse enthusiasts not to look directly at the Sun - with even brief exposure causing lasting damage - and to seek out specialist glasses instead.

But online, pairs that meet safety specifications have all but sold out. Those still available either require a hefty next-day delivery fee or simply cannot arrive on time.

Even the Royal Museums Greenwich - recommended as a reputable retailer by UK health officials - has sold out, citing an "unprecedented volume" of orders.

Meanwhile, eclipse glasses have been turning up for sale in unexpected places as retailers try to capitalise on the demand.

"I Googled 'where can I get eclipse glasses but not through the post', because I realised I was too late," one customer waiting to buy three pairs at the bakery on Monday tells BBC Radio 4's PM programme.

"People have been struggling to find them all over," says another.

With around 90% of the Sun set to be obscured by the Moon, the UK is expecting its most significant eclipse in 27 years.

The right glasses should have the international safety standard ISO 12312-2 printed on them, the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) has advised, and the lenses should not be scratched, torn or damaged.

It has also advised buying a new pair rather than using ones from 1999, and to take caution when it comes to glasses being sold online as the scramble for safe spectacles has prompted eclipse chasers to trawl social media for tips.

News.title: Watch: Family narrowly escapes home during Colombia earthquake
News.content:
A family captured video of the moment they fled their home during an earthquake in Colombia.

Liliana PÃ©rez Ocampo and her family escaped moments before their home was rocked by a 7.4 magnitude quake on Monday.

"At first, we thought it was just a mild tremor like the ones that usually happen in Colombia, but when more than 30 seconds passed and everything was shaking harder, we realised it was an earthquake," the mother-of-four told the BBC World Service.

Her family, including two young children at school, are safe.

"In the end, material things can be replaced," she said. "The most important thing is life, and we have that."

With at least 169 people killed, this has been the strongest earthquake to hit Colombia in the 21st Century, according to the country's Geological Service.

More on this story.

News.title: Anne Hathaway pokes fun at 'fake baby bump' theories
News.content:
Anne Hathaway has poked fun at those who suggested her baby bump didn't look real after a recent film premiere, telling them she had "fake hair, real bump".

The US actress turned heads in an outfit that showed off her bare bump at the launch of her new film, The End of Oak Street, in Los Angeles on Sunday.

It sparked a flurry of comments on social media, external from people saying "Why does it look fake?" and "Oh come on. That is not real." But others leapt to her defence, with one writing: "A lot of people in these comments have never seen a pregnant belly on someone who has abs."

Hathaway, 43, announced in June that she is expecting her third child with husband Adam Shulman.

News.title: Councils to get more powers to stop vape and betting shops, PM announces
News.content:
New vape shops will require planning permission and councils will get more powers to block new betting shops, under government plans aimed at improving high streets.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said town centres had been "hollowed out" by decades of decline and for many people, the high streets they grew up with are "unrecognisable".

He said the plans were "shaped" by a series of BBC News investigations which exposed organised crime on high streets, revealing shops selling illegal cigarettes, vapes, cannabis and cocaine, enabling illegal working and suspected money-laundering.

The Conservatives and Reform said the proposals would lead to "more empty" shops, without tax relief for other small businesses.

Burnham said the measures will give councils more power to control what businesses open in town centres.

The proposals come as the prime minister embarks on a tour of the UK, with Downing Street saying he will be in "listening mode" during his visits as he works on a "10-year plan to bring back hope".

The plans announced by the government include:

Changes to planning law which would mean every new shop selling e-cigarettes, or vapes, would need to apply to their local council for permission to open (England only)

Tightening the definition of a vape shop to prevent businesses avoiding the rules by describing themselves as a general convenience store or retailer (England only)

Scrapping a rule known as "aim to permit", which currently restricts councils' ability to refuse new betting shops and 24-hour slot machine shops (Great Britain-wide)

Requiring planning permission for new adult gaming centres, which offer 24-hour access to gambling machines (England only)

New powers to extend closure orders for mini-marts and vape shops found to be selling illegal tobacco or up to twelve months, something previously proposed by former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer (England and Wales)

The National Crime Agency (NCA) estimates that at least Â£1bn of criminal cash is laundered through high street stores in the UK each year through businesses connected to the sale of fake goods, tax evasion, illegal working and illegal drug supply.

Burnham told the BBC that the changes would make it "easier for police to close a vape shop and have it closed for longer".

He said: "At the same time we're changing the planning regime... which should stop the proliferation of vape shops on our high streets."

The prime minister added that Operation Vulcan in Cheetham Hill, Greater Manchester, cleared the area of counterfeits and crime and "proved" what could be achieved.

"When I look at police reform across England, I will be asking for a similar approach to be taken," he said. "I want the strongest possible neighbourhood policing, with all agencies involved, to rip out criminal behaviour that is pulling places down."

Burnham said he did not accept the decline of the high street as "inevitable".

"I don't see why anywhere should have to accept they have empty shops, vape shops and the challenges that come with that."

Housing Secretary Angela Rayner told BBC Breakfast on Tuesday that many people were frustrated at vape and gambling outlets "popping up even near schools and some of them are linked to illegal activity and crime".

News.title: Call with No 10 gives us hope, PC Harper's mother says
News.content:
Cole and Bowers were sentenced to 13 years for manslaughter in 2020. Under changes to the Sentencing Act made this year, they will become eligible for release from custody next January.

They are in a category of prisoners - those who have committed certain serious violent or sexual crimes - who until now would have had to serve at least two-thirds of their sentence in jail before being considered for release.

Downing Street had earlier warned it would not be possible to exclude "one or two offenders" convicted of manslaughter from the early release scheme.

However, the BBC has been told that Burnham has now instructed his justice secretary to find a way to exclude Cole and Bowers from the scheme designed to ease prison overcrowding.

In a later statement, the PM said he was "increasingly confident" that work to increase space in the prison system "will allow us to reduce the number of people released early".

He added: "And, in the case of the most serious offenders like those convicted of the killing of PC [Andrew] Harper, prevent their early release altogether."

Adlam said the conflicting reports had been making her "more and more angry" and the uncertainty had left her family "in turmoil".

Of the phone call she received, she said. "I think the fact it's actually come from Downing Street, I've got to try and have some faith in it, but at the same time I've got to protect my own feelings."

Thames Valley Police officer PC Harper, 28, from Wallingford, Oxfordshire, died in 2019 when he was dragged behind the getaway car of three teenagers who had fled the scene of a quad bike theft in Berkshire.

Adlam said: "Everybody is watching this. This is obviously extremely personal to us but it's to do with the country as a whole really. This is really vital to get right, it feels like a hash, like a rush job."

Speaking about Cole and Bowers, she added: "They weren't given extreme sentences and I'm only asking for them to do what they were given, I'm not asking for anything more than they were sentenced."

News.title: England set to be one of the first countries to eliminate hepatitis C
News.content:
Hepatitis C is spread through contact with blood infected with the virus, such as by sharing needles with someone who has it.

Donor blood is already screened for it.

It is a silent disease, meaning people often have no symptoms until much later.

Untreated, it can cause serious and potentially life-threatening liver damage.

NHS England says that since 2015, more than 100,000 people have been diagnosed and treated for hepatitis C, meaning the country is already meeting that target.

Another goal - a 65% reduction in hepatitis C-related mortality compared with 2015 levels - has yet to be met, but might be before the 2030 target date.

Around 50,200 adults are living with hepatitis C, figures for England in 2024 suggest.

Estimates indicate 84.6% of those living with hepatitis C have been diagnosed - just short of the 90% target.

The Hepatitis C Trust says England is "on the cusp" of one of the most significant public health achievements in our country's history.

Prof Frankie Swords, NHS national medical director, added: "England is now leading the world in the mission to eliminate this disease and on course to beat the WHO's 2030 target, but we are determined to keep up the momentum and finish the job.

"We are committed to finding and treating everyone who needs support and would urge those at greater risk to come forward by ordering a free and confidential home-testing kit online."

Adults born in Ukraine, Romania, Estonia, Latvia, Poland, Albania, Lithuania, Bulgaria, Czechia or Slovakia are particularly urged to test, as some may have been infected through medical or dental procedures before 1991.

People can order a free, confidential NHS home self-testing kit, external without needing to speak to a GP.

News.title: Perseid meteor shower reaches peak: When and where to catch a glimpse
News.content:
The best annual meteor shower has once again returned to our skies, and the Perseids dazzling display is set to peak on Wednesday night.

But skywatchers will be treated to not one, but two, impressive astronomical events within just a few hours of each other.

A deep partial solar eclipse will be also visible in the UK in the early evening before the Sun sets and the stars emerge. While the two events are unrelated, their timing makes for an exceptional night of stargazing.

Astronomer Dr Becky Smethurst said it was "the perfect cosmic coincidence of events".

Here is when to look up and where you will have the best views of the meteor shower.

News.title: London Heathrow no longer Europe's busiest airport
News.content:
Heathrow has lost its position as Europe's busiest airport to Istanbul, new figures show.

The west London airport said 7.86m passengers passed through its four terminals in July, whereas Istanbul Airport in Turkey's largest city recorded 8.15m passengers.

The US-Israel conflict with Iran has had an impact on Heathrow's passenger traffic with Middle East routes in July down 20.2% year-on-year.

Annual figures from trade body Airports Council International show Heathrow was Europe's busiest airport from 1996 to 2019. It lost that title in 2020 amid coronavirus travel restrictions before regaining it in 2023, holding it ever since.

Heathrow continues to operate its two runways at near-full capacity and is seeking government permission to build a third.

News.title: Antisemitism towards Jewish children 'shocking', government expert tells BBC
News.content:
Headteachers of some Jewish schools are spending more of their time dealing with security arrangements than on educational matters, a review into antisemitism in schools and colleges has found.

Sir David Bell, speaking for the first time about his ongoing government-commissioned independent review, told the BBC he had been struck by how many leaders of Jewish faith schools had told him security was their main concern - and that "sometimes education takes second place to that".

The extent of antisemitism directed at children and young people was "shocking" he said.

The report, due ithis autumn, examines experiences of Jewish pupils and staff in faith and secular schools and colleges in England.

Sir David said he found that pupils were "subject to regular harassment and abuse".

He said Jewish children and young people "are facing a pressure - and indeed one might say even a crisis - that is not the experience of other communities in this country".

The review is likely to recommend dedicated training for all teachers and improved education about antisemitism for pupils, the BBC has been told.

The BBC has spoken to several headteachers and staff at Jewish schools. All asked not to be named because of concerns over their security and that of their schools.

One headteacher said: "In recent years [security] has become an overwhelming priority and increased a significant amount. There have been weeks where approximately 90% of my time has been spent on security-related matters.

"Security concerns can become one of the many things that headteachers carry with them beyond the school day and, quite literally, can be among the things that keep me awake at night."

News.title: Girl, 6, dies and another child hurt in A12 crash
News.content:
A six-year-old girl was killed and another child was injured in a collision that shut part of the A12 on Monday, police have said.

The crash, involving a lorry and a car, happened at about 10:30 BST on the northbound carriageway near the Colchester United football stadium.

The road was shut in both directions and an air ambulance landed, while vehicles caught in the closure were turned around.

Det Insp Mark Fraser, of Essex Police, said the lorry driver had passed all road-side tests and was due to be interviewed in the coming days.

The injured child suffered a leg injury and was recovering in hospital, the force added.

The collision led to parts of Colchester being gridlocked throughout the day, while A12 queues stretched back to Marks Tey.

News.title: Murder accused X Factor singer gets legal deadline
News.content:
A former X Factor finalist accused of murdering a woman by running her over with a car in central London has been given seven days to confirm who will represent her at her trial.

Gabrielle Carrington, 29, denies killing Klaudia Zakrzewska outside the Inca nightclub in Soho on 19 April. Zakrzewska, 32, died from her injuries six days later.

It is alleged a woman got into a car before it lurched forward and hit Zakrzewska.

Carrington, from Manchester, appeared at the Old Bailey and told the court it would be "crazy" to represent herself and said she would confirm her chosen legal firm by 17 August. She was not represented in court by a barrister on Tuesday afternoon.

News.title: Two in court over teens' Thailand drug courier case
News.content:
Two people accused of trafficking teenagers to Thailand as part of an international drug ring have appeared in court.

Tremaine Jeanne and Jessica Sani, both 28, are charged with drug offences and conspiring to arrange the travel of another with a view to exploitation.

It is alleged they used two 17-year-olds as drug couriers after they were caught with 64kg (141lb) of cannabis in their suitcases while travelling back to the UK.

The teenagers from Cardiff, were arrested in Thailand in June and remain in custody. They are being supported by the Foreign and Commonwealth Office.

Four other people appeared at Cardiff Magistrates' Court last Friday in connection with the case.

A 23-year-old man from Keighley, West Yorkshire, who was also arrested on suspicion of improper importation of controlled drugs, has been bailed.

Jeanne, from Llanrumney, and Sani, from Newport, are both charged with conspiring to fraudulently evade a prohibition on the importation of a Class B drug and four counts of conspiring to arrange or facilitate the travel of another person with a view to exploitation.

They appeared via video link and spoke only to confirm their names, dates of birth and addresses. They were not asked to enter pleas.

Jeanne and Sani were remanded in custody and will next appear with their co-accused at Cardiff Crown Court on 4 September.

South Wales Police officers were told in June the teenagers had been arrested, and launched an investigation into the "circumstances" behind their trip.

A spokesman for the force said: "The children remain in custody in Thailand where they are being supported by their families and the Foreign and Commonwealth Office.

"The families have been updated regarding the arrests and charges."

News.title: Charlotte Church's forest school set up without permission on pig farm faces closure
News.content:
A forest school set up by singer Charlotte Church on a former pig farm might have to close because of environmental fears.

The Awen Project opened in 2024 without planning permission in Wenvoe, Vale of Glamorgan.

The singer, who appeared on series one of Celebrity Traitors, applied for retrospective permission in October 2025, but that was refused.

The council raised concerns over the noise, impact on residents, and dangers to pedestrians because of insufficient parking. It also said the project failed to show how it would "conserve and enhance green infrastructure".

Church refused to comment, but has appealed to the Welsh government's Planning and Environment Decisions Wales (PEDW).

The Awen Project aims to give children an environment "where they feel championed to be themselves and follow their passions as active participants in a democratic community".

The school is free and accepts donations.

It was originally based in Cwm George and Casehill Woods, near Dinas Powys, with permission from the Woodland Trust.

But, in 2023, the charity revoked the license agreement because of "multiple breaches" of the permission granted which "posed health and safety concerns" for "visitors and wildlife".

In response, the project posted on social media that it had given its "best efforts to salvage" the partnership.

A council spokesperson said the application was refused because of "concerns regarding the sustainability" of the site's location and the "potential impact on neighbouring residents was another consideration".

There was also "insufficient supporting evidence to satisfy concerns around the potential impact of the proposal on biodiversity and the natural environment", the council said.

PEDW confirmed it had received the appeal, but said no date has been fixed for the hearing.

News.title: Murder arrest over fatal shooting in Clapham
News.content:
A man has died in a shooting in south London and police have arrested a suspect on suspicion of murder.

Officers and paramedics were called to Willington Road, Clapham, just before 22:00 BST on Monday following reports of gunshots near The Landor pub.

A 25-year-old man was pronounced dead at the scene, the Metropolitan Police said.

Shortly after the shooting, a 22-year-old man attended hospital with a gunshot wound. He was arrested and remains in hospital while police await an update on his condition, the force added.

News.title: Teenager lured to park before knifepoint robbery
News.content:
Two teenagers who robbed one of their classmates at knifepoint and shared footage of the attack online have been given suspended jail terms.

Zain Khan and Nahid Ali, both 19, lured the victim from Craven College in Skipton, North Yorkshire, to nearby Airedale Park on 6 March 2024, where he was threatened with a knife, beaten, and made to transfer more than Â£800 into Khan's bank account.

Both men, who are from Keighley, West Yorkshire, admitted robbery and Khan also admitted possessing a knife.

At Bradford Crown Court on Friday Khan was given a two year jail sentence suspended for two years, and Ali was given a 20-month sentence also suspended for two years.

Khan also received a nine-month sentence for possessing a knife, suspended for two years.

Both Khan and Ali were ordered to complete 240 and 200 hours of unpaid work.

Two other teenagers who were involved in the attack were dealt with at an earlier hearing and ordered to pay compensation.

The court heard how on the day of the attack, the victim had been to the college cafe with Khan, a fellow student who he believed to be a friend.

While there, Khan suggested they go to the local Morrisons supermarket to buy food.

New wildfires have erupted in Greece as the summer’s extreme heatwaves continue to create tinderbox conditions across Europe.

Just days after Greek firefighters gained control of a deadly blaze in the Attica region, around 200 are tackling new outbreaks southeast of Athens.

At least five firefighters have been killed fighting the fires that have gripped Greece in recent days.

Large parts of the south of the country are already at an “extreme” or “very high” risk of wildfires, with the risk zones expected to expand as temperatures reach 35C later this week.

open image in gallery Firemen rushed to a fire that broke out at a livestock facility near Kouvaras, south of Athens ( AFP/Getty )

Fires started by sparks from the electricity grid have reportedly been responsible for as much as 75 per cent of the land burned in Greece this year, according to data from the Fire Service’s Arson Crimes Directorate.

More than 30,000 hectares have been scorched so far, the European Forest Fire Information System (EFFIS) said.

Greek authorities declared a category 4 threat on Monday in several regions including Greater Athens, the Peloponnese, Crete and Attica.

It comes as Europe is suffering its hottest summer on record, with average temperatures 2.79C higher than the 1991 to 2020 average.

open image in gallery Bell firefighting helicopters have been deployed across the country ( AFP/Getty )

The blistering heat has led to 25,000 related deaths this year, according to Bloomberg research covering Spain, France, the UK, the Netherlands and Switzerland, exacerbating wildfires that have burnt more than 550,000 hectares of land.

It has raised questions over the safety of Greece’s energy infrastructure in fire-prone areas, especially with its prevention efforts having been significantly hindered by the stringent austerity programme last decade which saw major cuts to fire prevention staff.

Early investigations into the Attica fire suggested that it started in the region of Boeotia after sparks from conductors on a private network transmitting electricity generated by wind turbines to the main power grid, the eKathimerini website reported.

open image in gallery Firefighters battled a blaze in west Attica, near Athens, for five days ( Reuters )

The fire in Attica took five days to bring under control, with fast gusts of wind up to 130kmph enabling its rapid spread.

Two emergency workers were killed after two firefighting helicopters collided as they battled the fire, with one spinning and crashing to the ground in a fireball. It followed three deaths just days earlier, two in Crete and one in the southern Peloponnese port town of Gytheio.

On Friday, a Greek magistrate ordered the pretrial detention of the mayor of Stylida, along with a contractor and a business owner that were tied to a wind farm project in Viotia, as they investigated the cause of the fire, eKathimerini reported.

A nationwide investigation into wind farms has been ordered by Greek prosecutors following the Attica fire, which will look into whether the farms are operating with the necessary permits and are following the rules governing their operation.

This year’s wildfires are not the worst on record in Greece, data according to the European Forest Fire Information System (EFFIS).

The 30,493 hectares that have so far burned pale in comparison with blazes in 2023 that torched 173,774 hectares, the 130,744 hectares in 2021 and 271,715 hectares in 2007.

open image in gallery Much of southern Greece, including around Athens, is at high risk of further wildfires this week ( AFP/Getty )

But the country remains vulnerable to devastating blazes, as a result of a decade of significant underfunding for prevention efforts, which could yet see the figure for this year significantly increase.

Forestry service officials told Reuters earlier this year that understaffing was hindering efforts to prevent fires or deal with ​their aftermath, after their funding was shrunk even as nearly 2.5 million acres of land have burned in Greece, according to government figures.

This was in large part owing to ​the austerity programme that followed a sovereign debt crisis last decade, with the number of staff dealing with fire prevention and mitigation more than halving since the year 2000 to fewer than 3,000 today.

open image in gallery At least five firefighters have been killed ( AFP/Getty )

Vangelis Gountoufas, director general of forests in Greece's environment ministry, said the industry has been “through a period of complete abandonment”.

Gountoufas said the government now recognises the problem. After more than two decades without permanent hires, the forestry service has added some 300 staff since 2024. Greece now seeks to catch up, using hundreds of millions in EU funding to pay for thousands of firefighters and equipment this decade.

“It is not always ​easy to fill within two or three years a gap made over two decades,” said Stathis Stathopoulos, who runs the forestry service at the ministry.

After a series of cyberattacks targeting America’s water infrastructure, a group of hackers have launched a program to help small, vulnerable water utilities across the country combat similar attacks.

DEF CON Franklin, a project from the Cyber Policy Initiative at the University of Chicago Harris School of Public Policy, has teamed up with the nonprofit group National Rural Water Association to open the Water Watch Center, which aims to provide direct support to water systems that routinely monitor and adjust safe drinking water across the country.

In recent weeks, water systems in at least 12 states — including more than 30 community water systems in Minnesota alone — were compromised by cyberattacks potentially stemming from Iran. Cybersecurity experts told The Independent last week that the new wave of attacks could open a new, asymmetrical front in the U.S. war with Iran that cash-strapped and under-resourced public utilities are not prepared to face.

DEF CON debuted its program at this month’s hacker conference in Las Vegas, following two years of work with roughly 450 volunteer hackers and cyber experts who paired up with water and wastewater utilities in seven states.

That work helped strengthen defenses in those states, but it also laid bare what the program describes as the “intractable problem” of scaling a national security model for the roughly 150,000 water and wastewater systems across the country.

open image in gallery A network of hackers and cybersecurity experts have launched a program to support the nation’s water utilities after a series of cyberattacks exposed dangerous vulnerabilities ( AP )

The Water Watch Center is now expanding that test model to support water utilities that serve fewer than 10,000 residents, accounting for the vast majority of the nation’s water infrastructure.

“DEF CON Franklin spent two years with volunteer hackers in the trenches with under-resourced water utilities analyzing data and testing hypotheses, many of which didn't work,” DEF CON founder Jeff Moss said in a statement.

“The result is a truly innovative, grassroots public policy program that only the hacker community would have come up with,” he said.

DEF CON Franklin, launched in 2024 and named after Benjamin Franklin, describes itself as a kind of cyber firefighting program that can address tech emergencies facing the nation’s critical infrastructure, including water systems and schools.

The latest attacks have prompted an urgent public response from cybersecurity experts who have sounded the alarms about vulnerabilities in the nation’s infrastructure for years with little action from state and federal governments.

open image in gallery President Donald Trump has dismissed reports from his own intelligence community suggesting Iran was behind the latest attacks, while cybersecurity experts are urging Congress to act swiftly to unlock federal support for cash-strapped local governments ( Getty )

Within recent weeks, “malicious cyber actors” infiltrated water systems and gained access to programs that monitor water pressure, chemicals and pumps, among other tasks, according to federal law enforcement agencies.

Hackers appear to have remotely accessed “programmable logic controllers” that are connected to the internet. The FBI and Cybersecurity & Infrastructure Agency have urged utilities to disable internet access, set up strong passwords and revert to manual control, among other changes.

The Operational Technology Cybersecurity Coalition said the attacks deserve more than a handful of alerts from federal agencies. “We must view this through a clear lens: an adversary has directly impacted a core American necessity,” the organization's executive director Tatyana Bolton wrote in an urgent appeal to members of Congress.

In March 2023, the Environmental Protection Agency under then-President Joe Biden published a memo requiring states to work with local officials to identify potential weaknesses in their water systems that hackers could exploit.

Attorneys general in three Republican-led states sued to block the policy, arguing that it exceeded the agency’s authority and unfairly placed the burden on improvements on cash-strapped states. The memo was later blocked by a federal appeals court, and the EPA then withdrew it.

Since taking office, President Donald Trump’s administration has also gutted the cybersecurity agency tasked with responding to similar threats.

The administration purged roughly one-third of the staff at the Cybersecurity & Infrastructure Agency, which has been villainized by the president and his allies over the agency’s past efforts to disrupt election disinformation.

Sen. Adam Schiff of California, the top Democrat on a water panel inside the Senate’s Environmental and Public Works Committee, filed legislation this week that would authorize the EPA to work on water cybersecurity issues — an attempt to enshrine into law what the Biden administration tried to do three years ago.

“These threats are not hypothetical — they are happening right now,” Schiff said in a statement Monday.

“This legislation gives EPA the tools it needs to protect this critical infrastructure while providing the resources that local water and wastewater systems need to strengthen their cybersecurity without passing the cost on to ratepayers,” he said.

DEF CON Franklin’s program has meanwhile developed a “scalable cyber delivery model that has eluded water industry and national security officials to date,” according to Jake Braun, co-founder of DEF CON Franklin and former White House acting principal deputy National Cyber Director.

With the program’s volunteer hacker army working alongside cybersecurity firms, “these folks walk in the door knowing the intricacies of cybersecurity in a water utility environment,” he said in a statement.

Rosario Dawson has spoken out about her filmed cameo in Spider-Man: Brand New Day that didn’t make the final cut.

The Star Wars: Ahsoka actor, 47, was originally expected to appear in the latest Marvel blockbuster as her Daredevil character Claire Temple/Night Nurse. But her scene was ultimately “cut out,” she revealed last month at GalaxyCon Raleigh 2026.

“I told my mom, and she was like, ‘That sucks. Now I can’t post the pictures,’ and I was like, ‘Right, mom, me being cut out of the movie that has like the largest viewership of a trailer ever, the issue is you can’t post your BTS photos,’” Dawson joked, according to The Wrap.

“When I tell you my post was already ready with my BTS, with like my grandson wearing all his Spider-Man stuff because he loves Spider-Man — then I got the email done,” she explained. “So yeah. I’m a reject of Spider-Man.”

Dawson starred as Claire Temple, a crucial medical ally and romantic interest to Charlie Cox’s superhero Matt Murdoch/Daredevil, in the three-season superhero drama Daredevil, which aired from 2015 to 2018. Daredevil and Spider-Man famously exist in the same live-action universe, with Cox even making a cameo in Spider-Man: No Way Home (2021).

open image in gallery Zendaya and Tom Holland reprise their roles as MJ and Peter Parker in ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ ( Sony )

open image in gallery Rosario Dawson filmed a cameo scene for 'Spider-Man: Brand New Day' that ultimately got cut due to time constraints ( Getty )

“I would love — I still, because everybody’s in it, it still means that my character is somewhere in that same universe, and I really love that,” Dawson said. “So I hope I get to be Claire again.”

The deleted Brand New Day scene showed Claire helping Tom Holland’s Peter Parker/Spider-Man into the hospital after his fight against Scorpion (Michael Mando), according to The Wrap.

Screenwriters Chris McKenna and Erik Sommers previously confirmed to the outlet that Dawson’s scene was likely removed due to runtime constraints.

“Rosario Dawson is great. I wasn’t there for those discussions. But it was great. If anything, you have a movie that is two-and-a-half hours long, and it’s almost an embarrassment of riches with so many great characters and so many great scenes,” McKenna said.

open image in gallery ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ is out now in theaters ( Sony Pictures )

“The scene they did was a good scene; I think the only reason it’s not in the final cut was just it was probably cut for time because it was very good,” Sommers added.

Spider-Man: Brand New Day marks Holland’s fourth solo outing as the web-slinging superhero, alongside Zendaya. The new film, which also stars Sadie Sink, Jon Bernthal and Jacob Batalon, is both a critical and massive box-office success, having earned $1.6 million globally in its second week.

“This is the best Spider-Man movie in more than 20 years,” The Independent’s Clarisse Loughrey boldly proclaimed in a four-star review.

More than 2,000 people have now died of Ebola in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), with the outbreak continuing to outpace the response because it spread for months undetected before being declared.

Government data shows the outbreak has recorded a total of 4,381 confirmed cases. The ongoing outbreak has so far had a case fatality rate of 45.9 per cent, more than the 39.6 per cent rate recorded in the 2014-2016 West Africa outbreak, which infected more than 28,000 people and killed at least 11,000.

That makes this outbreak the fastest growing in history. It actually began in February, the World Health Organisation (WHO) has said. It was not officially declared until 15 May, meaning there was a significant lag in containment efforts.

As a result, the virus remains “ahead of us”, a WHO official said during a press briefing as the death toll continues to gather pace. The first 1,000 deaths were recorded over nine weeks, but the second took just three weeks.

Early cases were wrongly attributed to malaria, typhoid or a more common type of Ebola, but genetic sequencing timed the outbreak as earlier than had been thought.

Aid agencies have warned that fear of infection and misinformation have also kept people away from seeking care, while the outbreak has disrupted essential healthcare services like routine vaccination and child birth.

“One doctor told our team that before the current outbreak, his facility saw an average of 500 patients a month but that has dropped to almost nothing,” said John Agbor, UNICEF’s representative in the DRC.

At more than 4,300 confirmed cases, the outbreak has caused eight times more cases than were recorded during the same period of the West Africa outbreak, which was caused by the Zaire strain of the virus.

The rare Bundibugyo virus responsible for this current outbreak has no approved vaccines or treatments.

The WHO warned that there is a need to “urgently intensify” response efforts because the virus continues to spread and too many patients are receiving treatment too late.

“Village centres outside of Bunia, they don’t have these services,” said Dr. Mohamed Janabi, WHO Regional Director for Africa, referring to treatment centres. “As a result, everyone comes to Bunia. Unfortunately, they come late.”

More than two-thirds of Ebola deaths are happening in the community rather than in treatment centres.

Between April and June, there was a 42 per cent drop in the use of essential health services in outbreak hotspots, according to UNICEF.

The outbreak is unfolding under extremely challenging conditions, with local health workers striking over pay, conflict from rebel groups as well as mass displacement and widespread misinformation that Ebola isn't real or is spread by aid agencies.

Response efforts have also been hampered by abrupt cuts to international aid, which have heavily impacted health programmes in already vulnerable countries like the DRC and disease monitoring.

In 2018, the US Agency for International Development (USAID) coordinated efforts to train thousands of local health workers, conduct contact tracing, increase laboratory capacity to test for Ebola, and vaccinate people against the disease. The July 2025 dismantling of USAID saw the vast majority of projects terminated.

Studies have been planned to find out if the virus is actually mutating, contributing to the severity of the outbreak, officials have said.

Clinical research trials are also currently underway on the use of MBP134 and Remdesivir to treat the Bundibugyo virus strain.

The Independent is preparing to publish its third annual Climate 100 List, as the world continues to break records for high temperatures and is suffering more extreme weather and wild fires.

This year is set to be even hotter than last, with unprecedented drought across the UK and wildfires affecting large swathes of Europe, the US and Canada, driving home the urgent need to tackle the climate crisis.

Lord Deben, the former chairman of the UK’s independent Climate Change Committee, wrote recently in The Independent that "for the first time ever the British military has warned the government that climate change and the damage we have done to nature seriously threatens our national security", and urges the government to act now.

Already, the UK has faced multiple heatwaves this year, resulting in schools and nurseries closing, much of the country under a hosepipe ban and “tropical nights”, where the temperature doesn't drop below 20C. According to research from Greenpeace, the UK has become a nation "fundamentally unequipped to cope with rising temperatures caused by climate change".

Around the world, America has seen heatwaves affecting 50 million people, with temperatures up to 40C (105F) and wildfires across France and Spain have forced hundreds of thousands to evacuate.

The writing is clearly on the wall, but there's still a long way to go, which is why The Independent is continuing to be at the forefront of calling for climate action, and has long reported widely on the climate crisis' many facets during its now 40 years of publication.

The Climate 100 List celebrates 100 changemaking people from around the globe who are finding positive climate solutions across industries including agriculture, science, business, entertainment and tech.

As well as those who have dedicated their lives and careers to fighting the climate crisis, it champions people in grassroot movements and startups to amplify their voices and work to The Independent's global audience.

The list will be unveiled alongside The Independent's Climate 100 event, held in New York on 22 September and hosted by The Independent’s Editor-in-Chief, Geordie Greig. It will feature a keynote speech by former British foreign secretary David Miliband. Mr Miliband is now president and CEO of the International Rescue Committee (IRC) and oversees the agency’s operations in more than 40 crisis-affected countries.

"For 40 years, The Independent has led the way in reporting on the climate crisis," said Geordie Greig, Editor-in-Chief of The Independent. "The Climate 100 List continues this work, and I am hugely proud of how it has grown in reach and ambition each year."

"At a time when governments and businesses around the world are backing out of climate commitments, it's crucial that inspiring individuals taking action are celebrated," said Zach Leonard, Executive Director of Foundation Development at The Independent. "Our Climate 100 list recognises these changemakers and highlights their work to a global audience – from environmental experts, to world leaders, to unsung heroes."

Each year, the list is compiled and reviewed by a dedicated team at The Independent, bar for five spots. These are left to our readers to nominate an unsung climate hero, making up the Reader's Choice section, which has been a key part of the list since its inception.

We know three out of four of our readers consider themselves to be environmentally friendly, and we want you to have your say, and once again we are asking readers to get involved and submit anyone they think deserves recognition for their positive impact on finding solutions for the climate. Whether it's a colleague, friend, family member, mentor or classmate – whoever it may be, we want to hear about the important work they're doing.

Off the coast of Cyprus, a bearded skipper named Pepis skilfully pulls two lionfish from experimental traps. He slices away their poisonous spines, prepares the catch, and drops them into a bucket.

The surrounding Mediterranean water appears completely still, offering little indication of the profound ecological shift taking place beneath the surface.

Pepis’ routine is part of a broader scientific effort to monitor and contain the influx of invasive species such as lionfish. Marine environments here are altering rapidly due to rising sea temperatures alongside the Suez Canal, which provides a gateway for species migrating from warmer tropical waters.

According to a survey compiled by the Cyprus Academy of Sciences, Letters and Arts – based on research from scientists across 11 nations – a new non-indigenous species is introduced to the Mediterranean roughly every fortnight. The report identifies over 1,000 non-native species in total, a notable rise from fewer than 800 recorded between 2012 and 2017 by the European Environment Agency.

open image in gallery The lionfish has no known predator in the Mediterranean and has a voracious appetite for native fish and crustaceans, scientists say ( REUTERS )

Experts highlight that these tropical arrivals from the Red Sea and beyond are pushing out indigenous marine life, altering natural food webs, and placing local fisheries under strain.

This underwater shift mirrors the severe impacts of climate change observed across European landmasses this summer, where extreme heatwaves, wildfires, and droughts have caused widespread disruption.

The development poses serious concerns for conservationists: although the Mediterranean represents just 0.8 per cent of global ocean surface, it holds as much as 18 per cent of all marine species worldwide.

"Changes have been drastic, especially since 2000," said Periklis Kleitou, a marine scientist at the Cyprus-based Marine and Environmental Research (MER) lab which is looking at ways to reduce the impact of invasive species.

"We see more and more non-indigenous species proliferating and dominating the marine environment and, unfortunately, fewer native species."

With a distinct spiky crest and permanent frown, the lionfish resembles an underwater punk. Lacking natural predators in Mediterranean waters, it consumes native fish and crustaceans in large volumes.

open image in gallery Scientists are looking for ways to adapt and one option is to get consumers used to eating new types of fish ( REUTERS )

To address this, MER is trialling specialised traps near Cyprus designed to capture lionfish and Atlantic blue crabs while permitting indigenous species to escape unharmed.

Similar ecological disruptions are occurring off the coast of Greece, where over 230 non-native species have been documented in recent decades, according to Paraskevi Karachle, research director at the Hellenic Centre for Marine Research.

These non-native animals affect ecosystems in distinct ways. Rabbitfish consume significant amounts of algae, stripping underwater habitats bare and competing directly with local plant-eating fish species, Karachle explained.

Meanwhile, the carnivorous Lagocephalus pufferfish – also known as the silver-cheeked toadfish – carries toxins potentially lethal to humans. It preys on native fish species and has been linked to declining octopus catches. Recognisable by its bulging eyes and buck teeth, it features a silver body covered in black spots.

Scientists turn to unique solutions

To control populations, authorities in both Greece and Cyprus have introduced financial rewards for fishers who land pufferfish.

"Invasive species are taking over our seas, and that affects the local biodiversity as well as the economy," said Christina Kakoulli, a marine biologist at MER.

Researchers are exploring practical adaptation strategies, including promoting non-native fish as viable food sources. Once stripped of venomous spines, lionfish is safe to eat; skipper Pepis suggests lightly flouring the fish before frying it.

"In the beginning people were afraid, but now they understand it's a high quality, delicious fish," said Petros Yiangou, a chef who works with MER on Life Prometheus, a European Union-funded project that looks at ways to reduce accidental capture of sharks and rays, while encouraging ways to harvest invasive species.

open image in gallery Greek marine researchers have tested ways of removing toxins to turn pufferfish into fishmeal for farmed sea bass and other research has explored possible uses in cosmetics, food supplements, leather products and pain relief ( REUTERS )

open image in gallery Ichthyologist Dr. Paraskevi Karachle holds bags made from pufferfish leather at the Hellenic Centre for Marine Research (HCMR) in Anavyssos, near Athens, Greece, July 28, 2026 ( REUTERS )

Commercial interest is already growing, with emerging markets for these fish in Lebanon and Turkey, while Tunisia has developed a market for Atlantic blue crabs.

In Greece, researchers have tested processing methods to neutralise pufferfish toxins, turning them into fishmeal for farmed sea bass, Karachle noted. Other studies are investigating potential applications for alien species across cosmetics, dietary supplements, leather goods, and pain relief products.

Establishing practical uses for invasive life forms may prove far simpler than pinpointing a single cause behind their expansion. Scientists emphasise that managing the phenomenon requires continuous, long-term monitoring.

"The sea is very complicated," Kleitou said. "It has so many confounding variables interacting at the same time."

American media tycoon Ari Emanuel’s events firm Mari has struck a deal to buy West End theatre owner ATG.

Mari, which runs Hyde Park Winter Wonderland, said it has entered into a “definitive agreement” to buy ATG Entertainment from private equity firm Providence.

The companies did not disclose the value of the deal, but the Financial Times previously reported that the move could value ATG at about £4.5 billion.

ATG runs about 70 theatres globally, predominantly in the UK and US.

open image in gallery Mari runs events including Hyde Park Winter Wonderland (Ben Stevens/PA) ( PA Archive )

The company, which has been owned by Providence since 2013, runs 10 venues in London’s West End, including the Lyceum, home to The Lion King, and the Savoy Theatre, which is staging Paddington The Musical.

It also runs a raft of regional theatres, such as Liverpool Empire, Edinburgh Playhouse and Manchester Opera House.

Mari, which is backed by Apollo Global Management and RedBird Capital Partners, snapped up Secret Cinema’s parent company TodayTix last year.

Mari also runs a raft of UK events including Winter Wonderland, Big Feastival and Hampton Court Palace Festival.

Bosses said that ATG will continue to operate under its existing brand and leadership.

Mr Emanuel, founder and principal investor of Mari, said: “I’ve spent my whole career in entertainment, and I started out in theatre.

“I’ve seen the industry reinvent itself many times, but live has only grown more powerful. Nothing connects great talent with audiences more directly.

“ATG has built one of the world’s great theatre businesses around that experience. This is a long-term bet on where live goes next.”

Melanie Smith, global chief executive of ATG Entertainment, said: “Mari understands live entertainment and what matters most to ATG: our theatres, the people behind them and the relationships we have built with producers, artists and audiences.

“That makes Mari the right home for our next chapter. We look forward to this new era and thank Providence for their unwavering support over the past thirteen years.”

News.title: Madagascar forced to divide and share mpox vaccine as epidemic takes off
News.content:
Authorities in Madagascar are being forced to split single vaccines into fifths to try to protect as many people as possible during an ongoing mpox outbreak.

The method, known as “fractional dosing”, is authorised by the World Health Organization (WHO) in emergencies when there are critical vaccine shortages, but is not routinely recommended and carries a level of risk.

Madagascar, the African island with a population of roughly 33 million people, is currently battling its largest-ever outbreak of the virus formerly known as monkeypox, with at least 4,000 cases recorded so far.

Another one million people are thought to be at risk of contracting clade 1b mpox, a fast-spreading strain of the virus that emerged from the Democratic Republic of the Congo in late 2023.

High risk groups include sex workers, young children, and people living with HIV/Aids. Medical workers are also at risk.

“We have been given too few doses to protect the at-risk population; we were initially given 30,000 doses in May, and a subsequent 30,000 have just arrived at the end of July,” said Akhil Bansal, a doctor of internal medicine working on the mpox response in Madagascar and a policy fellow at the Centre for Global Development.

“However, we need to vaccinate more than one million people, so we have been “fractionally dosing”, or splitting vaccines, into fifths, to stretch the supply as far as we can.

“This is a somewhat established approach for vaccines, but even then, the number of doses we have is insufficient,” said Dr Bansal.

News.title: Sudan exodus threatens humanitarian catastrophe in Chad
News.content:
Trapped in a desert encampment in Chad, Abakar Adam, 70, dreams of returning to his small farm in neighbouring Sudan, nearby to the village where he was born.

But Mr Adam can’t go home.

Hidden from sight, he watched soldiers set fire to his farmhouse and slaughter his livestock three years ago. One month later, after resettling in the city of El Geneina in West Darfur he heard 40mm grenades rain down on hospitals while patients fought for their lives inside and witnessed civilians executed in the street.

Shortly after, a bullet from the rifle of a Rapid Support Force (RSF) soldier ripped through his gut, and he recalls how he struggled to pull his daughter from the blood-soaked sand after her eye was gouged out by a militiaman during their escape from Sudan.

Now, sitting outside his rotting, wooden shelter in eastern Chad, just 20 miles from the border with Sudan, he tells The Telegraph that he can’t forget the faces of the blind and disabled who he witnessed being thrown onto piles of hay and burnt alive.

Adam’s story is not unique and the refugee camp where he finds himself with tens of thousands of others is on the brink of collapse.

News.title: Arsenal lose second successive pre-season friendly after parading Guimaraes
News.content:
Premier League champions Arsenal continue their preparations for the new season as they take on Borussia Dortmund in the Emirates Cup. Arsenal beat Spanish side Athletic Bilbao 3-0 in the 2025 edition, with goals from Viktor Gyokeres, Bukayo Saka and Kai Havertz sealing victory. These sides met during the 2014/15 Champions League group stages, with both games being won 2-0 by the home side.

Arsenal beat Girona 4-1 just over a week ago but fell to a 3-1 defeat to Real Betis in Dublin on Wednesday night. Reflecting on that defeat, Mikel Arteta expressed his frustration at the way his side conceded the goals.

“I am disappointed with the result,” Arteta told Arsenal’s in-house media. “We are here to win football matches. We had some fantastic moments in the first half, the way we played, the way we opened them up. We have to score first, clearly, in the two chances that we had before the score.

“I am very disappointed in the manner that we conceded the first goal, the two giveaways leading to the other two goals. It is true that the finishing quality from them was exceptional, but to win a football match, you have to compete at a different level, especially in those areas of the pitch and that is the learning from today [last Wednesday].”

This is in fact Arsenal’s first game at the Emirates since being crowned Premier League champions, as they sealed the title with a game to spare, with that final match of last season being away at Crystal Palace. After today, Arsenal have two more games, including the Community Shield in a week’s time, before they kick off the defence of their Premier League crown at home against newly-promoted Coventry. The likes of Declan Rice, Bukayo Saka and Martin Zubimendi are still yet to return after their World Cup exploits.

Dortmund, led by Niko Kovac, finished second in the Bundesliga last season, 16 points off winners Bayern Munich. They have played four pre-season friendlies thus far, winning twice and losing twice. The likes of Karim Adeyemi, Julian Brandt and Niklas Sule have left the club this summer.

Team news to follow shortly.

News.title: Andoni Iraola: Liverpool cannot ‘sustain the level’ I want
News.content:
Liverpool 2 Monaco 3

Andoni Iraola has conceded that Liverpool cannot currently “sustain the level” he expects after his side squandered a two-goal lead for the second match in a row.

In the Spaniard’s first game at Anfield since becoming manager, Monaco fought back to win 3-2 by virtue of Paris Brunner’s late glancing header seven days on from Leeds United’s 4-2 victory in Chicago, emphasising Liverpool’s alarming lack of depth, particularly in defence.

“We played a good first half, especially a good 30 minutes. Right now we probably don’t have much more, in terms of the levels required to play like this. They deserved to turn around the game.

“We won the first two pre-season games, but the last two we cannot sustain the level we want for all of the game. As soon as we made some changes, players start to get tired and we cannot sustain that level. So, we have work to do.”

News.title: Chelsea’s feisty friendly ends in penalty shoot-out confusion
News.content:
Chelsea’s pre-season tour of South East Asia ends today with a match against Johor Darul Ta’zim in Malaysia. The clash comes barely 24 hours after the west Londoners beat AC Milan 3-0 in Jakarta, a much-needed win coming on the back of defeats against Juventus and Tottenham.

A fine volley from Moises Caicedo and a double from João Pedro either side of half-time led Xabi Alonso’s side to victory in the Indonesian capital.

The game was fairly even in the first half and looked set to head into the break level at 0-0 but Pedro’s header from Caicedo’s corner put Chelsea in front.

Alonso’s side then doubled their advantage seconds into the second half as Pedro scored his second, assisted by Pedro Neto.

Just minutes later, Chelsea had their third courtesy of a well-worked corner routine. Romeo Lavia’s delivery was met by Caicedo on the volley, with the Ecuadorian’s finish with the outside of the boot finding the bottom corner.

Today, the west London side face Malaysian powerhouses Johor at the Sultan Ibrahim Stadium, more on them later, but considering the tight turnaround from yesterday’s match today’s clash will provide a stern test.

“The idea, with the game against Milan and then one in Johor, was to arrive at this weekend with players not being ready for 90 minutes until now,” Alonso explained after the win in Jakarta.

“We wanted to have a logical progression in their loads; so we had our plan and we’ve stuck to that.

“We have another idea [against Johor]; that was decided yesterday [Friday]. The idea is that many young players were coming to have chances to play tomorrow. If not, we’d have been short, as playing two games in two days is quite intense. So we will need them.”

Stay here for all the team news and action with kick-off set for 1pm.

News.title: Israel’s mental health time bomb
News.content:
This month alone, three Israeli soldiers are reported to have died by suicide, two of them young women. It takes to 17 the number who have taken their own lives since the start of the year, a rate higher than at any point in the last 15 years.

The month was made worse by the news last week that the boyfriend of Liron Barda, who was murdered at the Nova music festival during the October 7 massacre, had died beside the grave of his sweetheart.

Bar Asraf, 30, was having trouble coping. He had recently told his mother he was struggling without his girlfriend, reportedly saying, “there’s no one who can replace her, no one to cheer me up”.

These high profile tragedies are but the tip of a mental health crisis that is sweeping Israel, according to data collected by Clalit, the country’s largest health provider.

The study found post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) in the general population had increased by 70 per cent in the wake of the October 7 attacks and subsequent conflict.

News.title: I’m a professional cleaner and I swear by this three-ingredient carpet stain remover
News.content:
However effective your vacuum cleaner, there will always be those unfortunate spills and baked-in stains that need closer attention. I run a commercial cleaning business and rely on a homemade paste to remove the most stubborn marks from my carpets (and deploy it after any accidents). It’s inexpensive and you will probably have the ingredients in your cupboards already.

It won’t achieve a deep clean, though. If you’re looking to tackle bigger areas and own – or can hire – a carpet cleaner, I also have some fail-safe advice to ensure a pristine finish.

Spot clean stains with a homemade paste

For small stains, this quick concoction is all you need. Simply mix the following ingredients together slowly until they form a paste:

Half a cup bicarbonate of soda

1 tbsp mild washing up liquid

1-2 tbsp of warm water

Avoid brightly coloured washing up liquids, especially if you have lighter-coloured carpets, as the dye may transfer onto the fibres. Before you start, there’s one step that applies to any carpet cleaning; always test your cleaning solution (homemade or otherwise) on a small, hidden area of flooring to check for colour-fastness and compatibility.

News.title: Wildfire forces thousands to evacuate in Canada
News.content:
A fast-moving wildfire in western Canada forced more than 20,000 people to evacuate on Saturday.

The fire in Bald Range, British Columbia, doubled in size on Friday night as Canadian officials declared a state of emergency.

It spread rapidly to cover about 23,500 acres, prompting evacuation orders across the province, including the districts of Summerland, Peachland and other areas to the west of Okanagan Lake.

David Eby, the British Columbia premier, told a press conference on Saturday that one fire official had compared the blaze to a “bomb going off”.

Sports.title: Man Utd include surprise injured star in pre-season squad 254 days since he last played a game
Sports.content:
MATTHIJS DE LIGT was all smiles as he took part in Manchester United training in Dublin.

The defender, 26, has been out since last November due to a back injury.



De Ligt’s last game came 254 days ago, in United’s 2-1 win at Crystal Palace on November 30.

The Dutchman underwent surgery in May in a bid to finally fully recover from the issue.



Prior to this week, De Ligt’s pre-season had been limited to doing rehab at Carrington.

But as he continues to step up his recovery, the towering centre-back joined up with his team-mates in Ireland as they prepare to take on Leeds in Dublin this evening.



De Ligt is not ready to play and won’t be involved in the match.

While he did train at United’s temporary Ireland HQ, De Ligt was not involved in the full session.

The former Juventus and Bayern Munich star remains expected to miss the start of the season.

This week’s trip will have allowed him to take part in valuable team bonding.



BEST FREE BETS AND BETTING SIGN UP OFFERS

De Ligt has made 56 appearances for United, scoring three goals.

His upcoming return will be a boost to boss Michael Carrick, who is yet to have had De Ligt available during the entirety of his time in charge.

Benjamin Sesko also joined up with United in Ireland having recently been sidelined by a shin injury.

The forward is unlikely to play against Leeds this evening.



But there is a chance that he could feature against AC Milan this Saturday in Poland, as United lock horns with former boss Ruben Amorim.

Sports.title: ‘I don’t know what they were smoking’ – Arsenal trolled by Premier League icon over failed Vinicius Jr transfer pursuit
Sports.content:
JOHN OBI MIKEL brutally told Arsenal fans that Vinicius Jr was “using them” during his transfer saga.

The former Chelsea midfielder said that the Real Madrid superstar treated the Premier League champions as pawns to secure a better deal.



Last week, Vinicius, 26, agreed a new six-year deal with the 15-time European champions despite many thinking he could move to North London.

Speaking on the Obi One podcast, Mikel said: “I don’t know what the Arsenal fans were expecting.



“You win the league after 22 years and then you all of a sudden think: that’s it, you’ve arrived, you’re one of the big boys again. No, you’re not.

“They’ve just been humbled because I said it, there’s no way Vinicius Jr is leaving Real Madrid to go to Arsenal, a club that’s won one title in 22 years.

“This guy wins titles, he’s won lots of titles at Real Madrid. He wants to win titles season after season, the Champions League, La Liga, competing year after year and winning those titles.

“He’s tasted what it feels like winning the Champions League, Arsenal have never won the Champions League. Zero.

Sports.title: Transfer guru Fabrizio Romano drops major hint he will RETIRE in bombshell Linkedin post
Sports.content:
FABRIZIO ROMANO has suggested a major career change in a cryptic LinkedIn post.

The Italian, 33, has relentlessly posted transfer news on social media for several years.



Romano’s exclusives this summer have included Tottenham’s shock swoop for Sandro Tonali and Ronald Araujo’s loan move to Liverpool.

Reflecting on his summer’s work, the transfer reporter suggested that he will soon be embarking on a new challenge.



An excerpt of his LinkedIn post read: “I’m probably not gonna continue into the transfer market industry as I’m doing right now for longer: it’s time to change the approach, the view… but this will be another topic soon, after the transfer window closes.

“But still, these numbers feel incredible.



“The adrenaline of the breaking story, the exclusivity, the unexpected-factor, from zero links at all to done deal… well, this will always remain unmatched for me.”

Romano’s reporting, and signature catchphrase “here we go”, has seen him gather nearly 30 million followers on X and just shy of 50 million on Instagram



Earlier this year, however, he suggested that he would trade in his followers for a girlfriend.

Asked by Diletta Leotta if he would make the swap, Romano admitted: “Yes. Because you can get 10 million followers in the next year or so. But a girlfriend is not easy at all.”

On what type of relationship he’d like, Romano added: “Permanent term, of course. Long term.

“No, no for sure. I already had [my] fun, it’s OK.”



Romano, who hails from Milan, also revealed that his busy routine has gotten in the way of relationships, continuing: “There are certainly many problems, many difficult schedules.

“But more than schedules, it is above all the management of the telephone.

“You know, maybe if you are there at dinner and there is news. But it’s my own wish.”

In 2022, Romano told Optus Sports that he sometimes gets just four hours of sleep per night during the transfer window.

Sports.title: Who is Jose Mourinho’s wife Matilde Faria and how many children do the couple have?
Sports.content:
JOSE Mourinho has been one of the loudest voices in football for more than 20 years.

But the woman who has the “biggest influence” on him has maintained a much lower profile – here’s everything we know about the serial winner’s wife and kids.



Who is Jose Mourinho’s wife Matilde Faria?

Matilde Faria has followed the Special One through Benfica, Uniao de Leiria, Porto, Chelsea, Inter Milan, Real Madrid, back to Chelsea, Man Utd, Spurs, Roma, Fenerbahce, a return to Benfica, and now a second stint at the Bernabeu.

Born in Angola, Matilde grew up in Setubal, the Portuguese port city south of Lisbon where Jose Mourinho was born and where a street now carries his name.



Known to family as Tami, she knew him as a teenager and married him in 1989, before he’d managed a professional side.

In May 2014, the same day her husband was named a United Nations World Food Programme (WFP) ambassador against hunger, Matilde was appointed a WFP Special Ambassador for school feeding, promoting the agency’s work providing free school meals to around 24million children a year.



Mourinho has been blunt about the pecking order at home.

In 2015, he told The Big Issue: “My wife and my son and my daughter have the biggest influence on me, that’s for sure. And why? Because they are the bosses and control everything in the house!”

He added: “When it comes to make big decisions – where to go, where to work, when to change – on this kind of thing they have a big influence on me.”



Did Matilde Faria stop Mourinho becoming England manager?

England sacked Steve McClaren after failing to qualify for Euro 2008, and Mourinho, freshly out of Chelsea, was in talks to replace him.

In 2014, he explained: “I was almost, almost, almost, almost England manager at that time. My wife was right. She told me not to take it.”

Asked how close he came, he held a pen above an imaginary dotted line and said: “This close.”

He continued: “[Frank] Lampard, [John] Terry, Joe Cole, everybody, was saying, ‘Come, come, come.

“My players said, ‘The guys from Manchester United and Liverpool call us and say to us: Tell your boss to come.’ I had lots of positive things to push me…



“I cannot wait two years for a big competition. I cannot be spending two years playing against Kazakhstan and San Marino.”

He added: “In the end, my wife was saying, ‘No football, no matches is not for you’.”

Fabio Capello got the job, while Mourinho went to Inter and won the Champions League.

How many children do Jose Mourinho and Matilde Faria have?

Mourinho and Matilde have two children – daughter Matilde, known in the family as Tita, was born in 1996, and son Jose Mario Jr, known as Zuca, followed in 2000.



In 2013, he had his wife’s and their two children’s names tattooed on his left wrist.

Both kids had a nomadic childhood tracking their father around Europe – Matilde said she attended 11 schools before university.

Jose Jr went into football, coming through the youth systems at Real Madrid and Chelsea as a promising goalkeeper before signing a two-year scholarship at Fulham in 2016.

Since leaving the Cottagers the following year, Jose Jr has been away from the game.

But reports suggest he aims to follow in his father’s footsteps and pursue a career in coaching.



His daughter did a master’s degree at the Conde Nast College of Fashion and Design in London and runs her own jewellery label.

She married property consultant Danny Graham on October 12, 2024, at the family estate in Azeitao near Setubal.

The couple met as teens in London, but it was almost a decade later that he popped the question during a holiday in Portugal.

Matilde told Vogue: “He got down on one knee on the beach just by my family’s place. It couldn’t have been more perfect.

“He had my brother in on it, which made it the biggest surprise, considering how hard I usually am to surprise.



“After it happened, we spent the evening at home with my family, had pizza and wine to celebrate, and called our friends and family to share the news.”

Manchester United are ready to move for Club Brugge left-back Joaquin Seys after seeing their advances for two other targets, including Lewis Hall, knocked back

View 2 Images Joaquin Seys has impressed for Club Brugge with Man Utd now keen

Manchester United are ready to open talks with Club Brugge about a £30million deal for left-back Joaquin Seys after being knocked back by two of their targets.

‌



The Red Devils have added two new faces in midfield but left-back is another area where they are looking to bring in reinforcements. It has proved challenging throughout the summer however with the club onto their third different target.

‌



The Belgian side are in no hurry to sell and have Seys under contract for another three years. They will not ease off their £30m price tag, but it Mirror Football understands United are strongly considering an opening bid.

‌



The 21-year-old is a regular for Club Brugge and forced his way into Belgium‘s World Cup squad, featuring in his country’s quarter-final defeat to winners Spain last month.

Man Utd preparing for four transfer exits as Michael Carrick green lights departures READ MORE :

United did have Newcastle's Lewis Hall on their radar after the ex-Chelsea man had enjoyed the best season of his career to date, but the Magpies are refusing to sell up.

Already this summer Newcastle have lost marquee players in Anthony Gordon, Sandro Tonali and Bruno Guimaraes. Hall is one of the leading lights and St James' Park bosses have refused to entertain his departure. United had ultimately been priced out whilst another target, young Spaniard Jorge Salinas, is poised to remain in La Liga.

‌



He reportedly remains fully committed to Racing Santander and "doesn’t want to leave" despite interest from Manchester and Barcelona. His manager Jose Alberto has grown tired with the incessant speculation regarding Salinas’ future during the summer window.

United currently have Luke Shaw as their first choice left-back, but he has struggled to remain fit throughout his career and, now into his 30s, the club are looking to future proof the position.

Manchester United are ready to trigger Jorge Salinas’ release clause - but face competition from Atletico Madrid for his signature. Salinas came through the ranks at Real Racing Club de Santander and went on to make his first-team debut back in 2024.

‌



The left-back has since impressed in Spain, and, as a result, has been linked with a move away. As well as Atletico and United, Salinas has also been linked with a move to Barcelona.

‌



However, according to Spanish publication Sport, Barca have no intention of paying Salinas’ €16m (£13.6m) release clause. United, though, are ready to trigger it to snap up the 19-year-old this summer.

‌



But in a twist, the report also claims that Atletico are waiting for Matteo Ruggeri to complete a move to Aston Villa before making a move for Salinas. It is claimed that Villa have agreed a €18m plus €6m bonuses (£20m) deal with Los Rojiblancos for Ruggeri, meaning United may have to act quickly.

Despite the continued speculation around Salinas’ future, Racing boss Jose Alberto Lopez claimed earlier this week that the defender, along with Gustavo Puerta, don’t want to leave the club this summer. He said: "Their professionalism doesn't surprise me.

Wrexham AFC co-owner Ryan Reynolds has given a brilliant response to a couple moving from the USA to Wales after falling in love with Wrexham. Jeff and Janice Ivy are making the move after watching the Disney+ hit Welcome to Wrexham.

The series follows the club following the takeover by Reynolds and fellow Hollywood star Rob Mac. The club are currently in the Championship and aim to make it to the Premier League.

Taking to social media, Reynolds reposted the story of the couple's move, along with a comment reading: "Thank god they didn't watch Chernobyl." The mini-series Chernobyl dramatises the story of the real-life 1986 accident at the Chornobyl Nuclear Power Plant in Ukraine.
