World.title: Katele turns on HH, accuses President of failing to protect political opponents
World.content:
Former Finance Minister Dr Katele Kalumba has launched a blistering attack on President Hakainde Hichilema, accusing him of failing in his constitutional responsibility to protect Zambians holding opposing political views and alleging that the political environment ahead of Thursday’s general election has deteriorated dangerously.

In a direct address to President Hichilema, Dr Kalumba said he was speaking only days before the August 13 election because he had become deeply concerned about what he described as abductions, deaths and attacks involving people expressing political opinions different from those of the government.

“Mr President, my name is Katele Kalumba. I’m speaking to you directly from the election day,” he said, before referring to his past relationship with the President. “I’m thankful for everything you did to me, and I’m sure you should be thankful for everything I did to you.”

Dr Kalumba said he would not publicly explain everything that had previously transpired between the two men, saying President Hichilema already knew what he was referring to. He instead turned his attention to the current political environment, placing responsibility for the protection of citizens directly on the President.

“What is happening now is not in the interest of our country, and I believe that you are at the helm of it. You are responsible as the President of the Republic of Zambia. You are responsible to protect the lives of every Zambian under the Constitution of the Republic of Zambia,” he said.

He questioned what the presidency meant if the Head of State could not guarantee the safety of citizens expressing political opinions different from his own or seeking to provide alternative leadership.

“I don’t know what your job is if you cannot protect the lives of Zambians who are expressing a different opinion from you, and to provide leadership different from you,” Dr Kalumba said.

The former minister then delivered one of his strongest personal attacks against President Hichilema, saying his previous perception of the President had changed considerably.

“I’m disappointed, because I thought you were a good man,” he said. “What I have found out now is a man who was pretentious, a man who pretended to be a good man.”

Dr Kalumba went further, using extremely strong language to characterise the President and alleging that the country had witnessed “abductions, death, strangulation” and other acts in the political environment surrounding the election.

He did not, in the recorded statement, provide specific cases or evidence directly linking President Hichilema to the alleged incidents. His allegations therefore remain claims made by the former minister and are not established facts.

Dr Kalumba also compared President Hichilema’s leadership with that of late former President Edgar Lungu, arguing that his experience of both men had left him with a harsher assessment of the incumbent.

“You are worse than Edgar Lungu,” he said.

He said he had at different times been close to both political leaders and claimed he understood former President Lungu from both a family and political perspective.

“I was close to Edgar Lungu at some point, as I was close to you. In fact, closer to him. I understand him better, from the family level to the political level,” Dr Kalumba said.

The veteran politician then revisited his involvement with President Hichilema during the 2015 presidential election campaign, saying he had worked as a campaign strategist for him and had believed at the time that he was making sacrifices in support of a man he considered a gentleman and a civilised political leader.

“But as a campaign strategist for you in 2015, which goes to be my business, my family’s business, I expected you to… I thought I was sacrificing for you, a gentleman, a civilised human being,” he said.

Dr Kalumba then made an extraordinary personal accusation against President Hichilema, claiming that allegations he had previously been accused of making about the President were now words he was prepared to state directly.

“Now I’m going to say it to your face,” he said, before accusing President Hichilema of believing in “nothing else than satanism.”

No evidence supporting that allegation was presented in the recording, and the claim represents Dr Kalumba’s own accusation against the President.

The former minister also claimed he had previously defended President Hichilema when there were attempts to arrest him in connection with what he referred to as “San International Hotel.”

“I was trying to defend you. I defended you when he said he wanted to arrest you over San International Hotel. I knew much, and I still do, but I defended you,” Dr Kalumba said.

He claimed that his intervention had helped President Hichilema avoid what he described as a “trap”, although he did not provide further details about the circumstances or identify precisely who he said was behind the alleged attempt.

“I made sure you got out of the trap and nobody exactly knew what I was saying,” he said.

Towards the end of the recording, Dr Kalumba also referred cryptically to Cape Town, saying: “I knew what had happened in Cape Town. I knew…”

The recording ends at that point without Dr Kalumba explaining what event he was referring to or providing further details.

The intervention represents a sharp change in tone from Dr Kalumba’s public assessment of President Hichilema earlier in the election campaign. In May, the former minister said President Hichilema remained politically ahead going into the August 13 general election, although he believed the contest was becoming increasingly competitive.

His latest remarks, however, move beyond an assessment of the electoral contest and amount to a direct personal and political attack on the President just days before Zambians vote.

The allegations concerning violence, abductions and other criminal acts contained in Dr Kalumba’s statement have not been independently substantiated in the recording, while President Hichilema and the UPND were not heard responding to the specific accusations made by the former minister.

With Zambia heading to the polls on Thursday, Dr Kalumba’s intervention adds another forceful voice to the increasingly charged final stages of the campaign, while leaving several of his most serious claims unexplained and unsupported by specific evidence in the statement itself.

World.title: Nakonde election preps advance
World.content:
Electoral stakeholders in Nakonde district in Muchinga Province have commended the Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ) for promoting transparency and ensuring peace during the preparations for Thursday’s general elections.

Nakonde Forum for Persons with Disabilities Chairperson, Martin Gondwe, thanked ECZ for exhibiting transparency and hoped this would be maintained throughout the electoral process.

Speaking in an interview with the Zambia News and Information Services (ZANIS), Mr Gondwe called on all political parties to preach peace in communities ahead of the polls.

Mr Gondwe further appealed for inclusion of persons with disabilities in the voting process and asked if braille tactile jackets will also be available during the verification exercise.

“Make sure you preach peace wherever you are going, in our camps. Persons with disabilities and women inclusive, we want to participate in a violence-free election this year,” he said.

And United Party for National Development (UPND) Chairperson for Nakonde District, Derick Banda, said the process had been peaceful.

He expressed optimism that the same peaceful mood will prevail as poll staff are deployed and dispatched to polling stations tomorrow.

He also expressed gratitude to other stakeholders who have been available from inception, to ensure transparency.

“So far so good, the process has been peaceful for us. The most important thing we always preach is peace. Even from the time we received the ballot papers it has been peaceful,” he said.

And National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity (NRPUP) Mwenzo Constituency Chairperson, Frederick Siame, called for continued transparency during the dispatch of poll staff and verification of election material.

Mr Siame also expressed satisfaction with how the election preparations have been conducted in the district.

“So far so good. As we do the verification exercise when dispatching poll staff, we need to verify what the contents are. What we are asking for is the same transparency that has prevailed to continue,” Mr Siame said.

World.title: ZAF, NAPSA, LWSC seal deal
World.content:
Ministry of Defense Permanent Secretary Maambo Hamaundu has described the signing of a contract for the design and construction of a bulk water pipeline system for several housing developments in Lusaka as a significant step towards improving access to reliable water supply.

The pipeline will serve Kingsland Housing Estate, Zambia Air Force Twin Palm Base, Datong and River View Park, respectively.

Speaking during the signing ceremony, Mr Hamaundu said the project underscores the beginning of a transformative development initiative, aimed at providing sustainable infrastructure and improving the quality of life for citizens.

He said the initiative demonstrates what can be achieved when government institutions and strategic partners work together towards a common national purpose.

Mr Hamaundu said the government remains committed to improving the lives of Zambians through deliberate investment in infrastructure, housing, water supply and sanitation.

He said access to clean and reliable water is a fundamental human necessity and an important driver of national development, as it supports public health, education, economic productivity, environmental sustainability and social well-being.

Mr Hamaundu said the project aligns with the government’s broader development agenda of ensuring that citizens have access to essential services that promote dignity, good health and economic opportunity.

He noted that improved access to safe water and sanitation can reduce disease outbreaks, improve productivity and make housing developments more attractive to investors.

Mr Hamaundu commended the multi-sectoral partnership involving the Zambia Air Force, the National Pension Scheme Authority (NAPSA) and the Lusaka Water Supply and Sanitation Company Limited.

Lusaka Water Supply and Sanitation Company Managing Director Jilly Chiyombwe said the project represents an investment of approximately 150 million kwacha by NAPSA through Sable Projects, will include the construction of about 12 kilometres of a 450-millimetre diameter water pipeline, a 1,000-cubic-metre ground reservoir and associated project infrastructure.

And NAPSA Acting Director General Joshua Malipenga described the project as an important milestone in efforts to provide sustainable infrastructure to support residential and commercial development in the rapidly growing area.

World.title: We will expand student loans-HH
World.content:
President Hakainde Hichilema says his administration plans to expand student loans, bursaries and meal allowances, to accommodate more students beyond just public universities.

President Hichilema has assured that his administration will continue to invest in the education sector as this will not only contribute to job creation, economic growth, but also increase national revenue.

The President said that once re-elected for a second term, he intends to introduce a student internship programme for students to be attached to various institutions, in order to help them secure jobs once they graduate.

The Head of State said this during an engagement with students from over 50 higher institutions of learning in the country, at State House, in Lusaka.

“It does not matter whether you are from a private university or public university because a student from a private university is no different from a student in a public university. Why? They are all citizens of Zambia”, he stressed.

The President also indicated that his administration has transformed education into an economic sector, in order to generate more income for the nation and support delivery of various services such as health and infrastructure, among others.

He noted various reforms scored by his administration in the education sector, such as the signing of free education into law, re-introduction of meal allowances, infrastructure development as well as distribution of desks.

Earlier, students’ representatives commended the government for various achievements scored in the education sector over the last four years, plus.

Nelson Nyirenda, a fifth year student at Levy Mwanawasa Medical University thanked President Hichilema for signing free education into law, increasing the Constituency Development Fund (CDF) and student loans.

And a representative from the National Council of Student Unions (NACOSU), Vincent Sakala noted that students and the health sector in the country are the biggest beneficiaries of CDF.

“Students are the biggest community in the country, sponsored by CDF. Come August 13th, we have resolved to give 5.8 million votes to President Hichilema”, he pledged.

Another Student of Levy Mwanawasa University, Brian Malambo expressed confidence that if given another term, President Hichilema would drive the country towards economic stability through his strategies aimed at boosting production.

World.title: Liberia: Boakai Names Retired Army General to Head Anti-Drug Agency
World.content:
The Executive Mansion says Ziankahn's appointment reflects the President's confidence in his "leadership, integrity, and operational experience."

President Joseph Nyuma Boakai has made perhaps his most consequential national security appointment since assuming office, naming former Defense Minister, retired Major General Daniel Dee Ziankahn, as Director General of the Liberia Drug Enforcement Agency (LDEA) in a move that signals a fundamental shift in the government's strategy against transnational narcotics trafficking.

The appointment comes at a defining moment for Liberia's anti-drug campaign -- one marked by record cocaine seizures, allegations of institutional infiltration by organized crime, dismissals of senior security officials, and mounting international scrutiny over whether Liberia has become an emerging transit and storage hub for global narcotics syndicates.

Rather than selecting another career drug enforcement officer, President Boakai has entrusted the agency to one of the country's most experienced military minds, suggesting that the administration increasingly views narcotics trafficking not merely as a law enforcement problem but as a national security emergency.

Ziankahn's appointment follows months of extraordinary anti-narcotics operations that have transformed Liberia's security landscape.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

The crisis reached international prominence after authorities intercepted approximately 237.6 kilograms of cocaine valued at about US$19 million at Roberts International Airport earlier this year. That operation exposed what investigators described as sophisticated trafficking methods involving airport operations and triggered an extensive criminal investigation.

Only weeks later, authorities executed an even more dramatic operation in Duazon, Margibi County, where investigators seized nearly 3.97 metric tons of suspected cocaine with an estimated international street value exceeding US$370 million -- one of the largest narcotics seizures ever recorded in Liberia and among the most significant in West Africa.

The scale of both seizures fundamentally altered perceptions of Liberia's role in international narcotics trafficking.

For years, security analysts had warned that West Africa was increasingly serving as a bridge between cocaine-producing regions in Latin America and lucrative consumer markets in Europe.

The Liberian seizures appeared to reinforce those concerns, suggesting that international trafficking organizations may have established increasingly sophisticated logistical networks within the country.

The investigations that followed produced consequences extending far beyond the drug seizures themselves.

As investigators traced the alleged trafficking operations, allegations emerged suggesting that elements within the security architecture may have been compromised.

President Boakai responded with an unprecedented series of administrative actions, dismissing, suspending and ordering investigations into officials from several security institutions, including the Liberia National Police (LNP), National Security Agency (NSA), Roberts International Airport (RIA), and the Liberia Drug Enforcement Agency itself.

Those measures reflected the administration's determination to demonstrate that no institution would be insulated from accountability if credible evidence of misconduct emerged.

The actions also exposed what many analysts consider the greatest institutional threat confronting the country's anti-drug campaign: the possibility that sophisticated international criminal organizations may seek to infiltrate state institutions responsible for combating them.

Such concerns are not unique to Liberia.

Across the world, transnational narcotics organizations have historically relied not only on logistical sophistication but also on corruption, insider facilitation and institutional compromise.

Why Ziankahn?

Against that backdrop, President Boakai's choice of Daniel Dee Ziankahn appears highly strategic.

Unlike many previous leaders of the LDEA, Ziankahn arrives with decades of experience in military command, institutional reform and national security planning.

During his tenure as Chief of Staff of the Armed Forces of Liberia (AFL), he became widely associated with efforts to professionalize Liberia's post-war military following years of civil conflict.

Working alongside international partners, including the United States, he helped oversee reforms aimed at transforming the AFL into a disciplined, professional institution operating under democratic civilian control.

His subsequent service as Minister of National Defense further expanded his experience managing complex security institutions and coordinating with regional and international partners.

More recently, Ziankahn has served as Military Adviser to President Boakai, providing strategic advice on national and regional security matters.

His appointment therefore brings together operational military leadership, institutional reform experience and direct presidential confidence.

Unlike a conventional law enforcement appointment, it places a seasoned strategic commander at the helm of the country's principal anti-narcotics agency.

The Executive Mansion emphasized that Ziankahn's appointment reflects the President's confidence in his "leadership, integrity, and operational experience," while assigning him direct responsibility for intensifying Liberia's campaign against illicit drugs and organized crime.

The President has also appointed to the LDEA Precious Rue as Deputy Director General for Operations and Prince Mulbah as Deputy Director General for Administration, pending Senate confirmation.

All three officials have been instructed to assume their responsibilities immediately in acting capacities.

The restructuring also returns Ernest Tarpeh to the National Security Agency, while former Officer-in-Charge Fitzgerald Biago has been indefinitely suspended from the Liberia National Police over ethical concerns pending further investigation.

Although the Ministry of Justice reportedly found no evidence directly linking Biago to narcotics trafficking, President Boakai concluded that ethical issues identified in the investigation warranted additional scrutiny.

That distinction reflects the administration's emerging message: legal innocence does not necessarily preclude administrative accountability where questions of institutional integrity arise.

Ziankahn's appointment inevitably raises broader questions about the evolving character of Liberia's anti-drug campaign.

Drug enforcement agencies traditionally operate as civilian law enforcement institutions emphasizing criminal investigations, prosecutions and intelligence gathering.

By selecting a retired four-star military officer to lead the LDEA, President Boakai appears to be elevating narcotics trafficking to the level of a national security threat.

That does not necessarily imply militarization of policing.

Rather, it suggests greater emphasis on intelligence coordination, operational discipline, inter-agency cooperation and strategic planning.

The President has directed the new leadership to work closely with the Ministry of Justice, Joint Security and international partners to dismantle trafficking networks, strengthen border controls and improve intelligence capabilities.

Such coordination will likely become increasingly important as investigations continue across multiple jurisdictions.

Liberia's response carries significance beyond its borders.

International partners -- including the United States, the European Union, the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC), ECOWAS and INTERPOL -- closely monitor countries serving as potential transit points for narcotics trafficking.

Major cocaine seizures often become tests of institutional credibility.

Foreign governments generally assess not only whether drugs are intercepted but also whether investigations reach the criminal networks responsible and whether compromised public officials are held accountable.

Close 

Boakai's successive dismissals, suspensions and institutional reforms therefore appear designed partly to reassure international partners that Liberia remains committed to confronting organized crime despite the scale of recent challenges.

Yet appointments alone cannot dismantle sophisticated international trafficking networks.

Experts note that sustainable success will depend on broader institutional reforms, including stronger financial investigations, improved border surveillance, enhanced intelligence-sharing, witness protection mechanisms, prosecutorial capacity and judicial efficiency.

Liberia must also continue strengthening airport security, maritime surveillance and anti-money laundering systems if it hopes to disrupt the financial infrastructure sustaining organized criminal enterprises.

Equally important will be restoring public confidence in institutions that recent investigations have exposed to allegations of misconduct.

Announcing the appointments, President Boakai reaffirmed that narcotics trafficking represents one of Liberia's gravest threats to national security, public health and national development.

"Our fight against drugs is a fight for the future of Liberia," the President declared. "We will continue to strengthen our institutions, hold public officials to the highest ethical standards, and pursue those who seek to poison our communities. There will be no safe haven for drug traffickers or those who aid and abet them."

Those remarks reinforce an earlier pledge made after the first major cocaine seizure that his administration would dismantle the criminal networks operating within Liberia rather than merely seize narcotics shipments.

The assignment, for Ziankahn, may become the most demanding chapter of a career spanning military leadership, defense policy and national security.

It also represents, for the President, a high-stakes bet that disciplined leadership, institutional credibility and strategic coordination can restore confidence in an agency whose reputation has been shaken by allegations of internal compromise.

World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - August 11, 2026
World.content:
Zambia Election Set for Closely Fought Opposition Battle

Zambia's 13 August election has become a closely contested battle between the ruling United Party for National Development and the Tonse-Pamodzi opposition alliance, led by newcomer Brian Mundubile and backed by former Patriotic Front structures. The election is expected to test the opposition's strength and serve as a referendum on President Hakainde Hichilema's record. The government has made progress on debt restructuring, economic growth and inflation. But the high cost of living remains a big concern for voters. The poll is also taking place amid concerns over alleged state interference, restrictions on opposition activity and controversial legislative changes, making it a key test for Zambia's democracy.

WHO Warns DR Congo Ebola Response Falling Behind

More than 1,900 people have died in the Democratic Republic of Congo's Ebola outbreak. 60-70% of deaths occur in communities before patients reach treatment centres. The WHO said that the concentration of healthcare services in Bunia, Ituri province, is forcing patients to travel long distances and seek care too late. Poor transport systems may also increase transmission. The agency plans to expand treatment facilities closer to communities, add 400 Ebola beds and strengthen public awareness and early referrals. WHO is also looking to the town of Aru, where no new cases have been reported for two weeks after authorities expanded surveillance and response beyond individual patients to surrounding communities.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Nigeria Lassa Fever Cases Reach 1,000 in 2026

Nigeria has reported 1,000 confirmed cases of Lassa fever and 237 deaths in 2026, with cases reported in 23 states and 116 local government areas. Five states, Ondo, Bauchi, Taraba, Edo and Benue, account for 86% of confirmed cases. At least 53 healthcare workers have also been infected, prompting the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention to introduce a 30-day protection plan for frontline staff. The agency has said that late presentation, high treatment costs, poor sanitation and limited awareness are contributing to the outbreak and high fatality rate. Lassa fever is a viral haemorrhagic disease transmitted primarily through contact with food or household items contaminated by the urine or faeces of infected rodents.

Malawi Land Audit Flags Irregular Plot Allocations

Malawi's Ministry of Lands is set to release findings from a pilot land ownership audit in Lilongwe that reportedly uncovered irregularities in the allocation of plots in the affluent Area 3 and Area 10. The audit was launched in February 2026 to improve transparency and accountability in land administration. It is said to have identified politically exposed individuals, including current and former ministers, judges and MPs, among those allegedly linked to irregular land acquisitions. The findings could trigger political controversy, with questions remaining over whether those implicated will be publicly named or face legal or disciplinary action.

UN Somalia Auction Raises Security Concerns

The UN Support Office in Somalia (UNSOS) has opened a tender to auction vehicles, generators, IT equipment, medical supplies, construction machinery and other assets. This comes as Washington moves to end funding for the mission's logistical support by the end of 2026. UNSOS provides critical transport, fuel, food and other supplies to about 12,000 African troops and police serving under AUSSOM in the fight against al-Shabab. The auction has raised concerns among civil society groups over transparency and oversight. Regional leaders have warned that any premature reduction in international support could create a security vacuum as al-Shabab continues to operate in parts of Somalia.

Close 

Climate Change Shifts Africa's Malaria Risk

Climate change is reshaping malaria risk across Africa, with rising temperatures making parts of southern Africa and high-elevation areas of East Africa increasingly suitable for transmission, according to a new Nature study. Some parts of West and Central Africa may have become too hot for optimal malaria transmission. The region still bears about 95% of the global malaria burden. But experts warn that climate change is only part of the equation, with funding gaps, drug and insecticide resistance, and weak health systems still major threats. They are urging countries in emerging risk areas to step up malaria prevention and surveillance while maintaining elimination efforts in high-burden areas.

World.title: South Africa: Immigrant Traders See Their Livelihoods Destroyed By March and March
World.content:
Traders with documents and permits chased away, leaving Bellville bus terminus market almost empty

Dozens of immigrant traders who usually traded at the Golden Arrow terminus in Bellville are staying away because of anti-immigrant protests.

When we visited the once bustling site last week, it was quiet with only a handful of traders. Many stalls were deserted.

Some traders we spoke to said they had tried to set up shop in other areas but were stopped. They have not traded at the bus site since the March and March 30 June "deadline" demanding "illegal immigrants" leave South Africa.



"I need to pay rent, put food on the table, and pay the bills," a Zimbabwean man who asked to remain anonymous told GroundUp.

He said he has been selling clothes in Bellville for about five years. He left Zimbabwe in 2008 when its economy collapsed.

While he has not been directly threatened, he has witnessed others being harassed.

"They will take your stuff and throw it on the ground," he said.

"It hurts, but as much as it hurts, it's their country, and they're also marginalised people."

Another trader, who introduced herself as Meye, said she has had a permit to trade since 2010. She fled the DRC in 2003.

"We are legal; everything is correct. But they say we are foreigners and we need to go back to our country."

A single mother of three, she says she is now struggling to feed and school her children.

Another single mother, Safia, says she has been unable to trade despite having refugee status and a trading permit. She came from Somalia in 2010.

She said law enforcement needs to protect the traders better.

"I can't sleep at night because of what is happening. I can't even pay my rent. I can't support my children," she said.

Abdulhakim Husein, Western Cape director of the Somalia Association of South Africa, told GroundUp that he had been assisting traders since the start of July.

He said many asylum seekers and refugees are traders as they have to rely on being self-employed. They came from Somalia, DRC, Zimbabwe, Angola and Burundi.

He said that at a meeting on 13 July (which the City confirmed), it was agreed that traders with valid permits should be allowed to trade. But on 14 July, they received a message warning them about a March and March protest in the area.

Husein said they have approached a legal NGO for assistance.

City spokesperson Luthando Tyhalibongo said foreign nationals whose immigration status has been verified by Home Affairs are permitted to trade with a valid permit. These cost R78 per month.

Close 

"It is a concern whenever permitted traders, whether South African citizens or foreign nationals lawfully permitted to trade, are prevented from engaging in legal economic activity," he said.

He said intimidation and threats should be reported to SAPS.

World.title: South Africa: Gauteng Gets 500,000 Grade 1 and 8 Applications - South African News Briefs - August 11, 2026
World.content:
Gauteng Records Nearly 500,000 Grade 1 and 8 Applications

Almost half a million applications have been submitted for Grade 1 and Grade 8 places in Gauteng for the 2027 academic year since the online application system opened, reports EWN. The Gauteng Department of Education has said that improvements have been made to streamline the process. Education MEC Lebogang Maile has urged parents to apply early. The department also says learners awaiting specialised placement should receive interim support rather than remain on waiting lists, with officials focusing on successful placements and resolving outstanding cases.

Strong Winds Damage Homes in Free State

The South African Red Cross Society is assessing damage caused by strong winds and heavy rainfall in Koppies and other parts of the Free State, reports SABC News. Several homes have reportedly been damaged, including roofs blown off, as severe weather persists. Red Cross volunteers are working with disaster management authorities and municipalities. Assessments continue, with humanitarian assistance being provided to affected households.

Fadiel Adams Unlikely to Testify at Madlanga Commission

National Coloured Congress leader Fadiel Adams is unlikely to testify before the Madlanga Commission, reports EWN. This comes after the commission received his affidavit and supporting documents late. Adams was expected to testify about his involvement in an Investigating Directorate Against Corruption probe into alleged corruption within Crime Intelligence. In 2024, he asked IDAC to investigate claims that the Political Killings Task Team had misused secret service funds for luxury accommodation and vehicles.

World.title: Somalia: UN Puts Somalia Mission Assets Up for Sale As U.S. Funding Cutoff Looms
World.content:
Mogadishu, Somalia — The United Nations Support Office in Somalia (UNSOS) has opened a tender seeking licensed auctioneers to sell off a wide range of its vehicles, generators and other equipment in Somalia, a notice published on the UN Global Marketplace shows.

The call for expressions of interest, issued August 6, comes as Washington moves to cut off funding for the UN's logistical support mission by the end of 2026, deepening uncertainty over the future of international backing for Somalia's fight against al-Shabab.

The tender matters now because it lands at the center of a widening rift between the United States and the United Nations over how and whether, to keep supporting Somalia's security transition. UNSOS underpins the African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia (AUSSOM), supplying transport, fuel, food and other non-lethal supplies to roughly 12,000 African troops and police fighting a resilient insurgency. Any wind-down of that support network would strike at the core of the mission's ability to operate.

Under the terms of the tender, UNSOS is looking to establish a local contract for the "commercial sale" of UN-owned property. The initial deal would run three months, with up to three additional three-month extensions depending on performance and operational need.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

The list of items up for sale is extensive: vehicles, generators, computers and IT equipment, office equipment, shipping containers, security watchtowers, wastewater treatment plants, prefabricated accommodation materials, medical and laboratory equipment, electrical appliances and heavy construction machinery. UNSOS said the list is indicative and may grow.

Interested firms have a narrow window to respond, with registration required by August 11 -- just five days after the notice was published.

Civil society analysts in Mogadishu have indicated that the auction notice does not lay out a clear mechanism for independent oversight, warning that disposing of mission assets without transparency could weaken public trust and open the door to diversion of state property.

The auction notice does not link the sale to the funding dispute. But it follows a July 1 letter in which the United States cited concerns over Somalia's performance against al-Shabab and its handling of security and governance issues, and comes as Washington has pushed back against extending UN logistical support for AUSSOM beyond current arrangements.

Somalia has fought al-Shabab for nearly two decades, and the group still holds sway over parts of the country. Leaders of AUSSOM troop-contributing nations have warned that a premature drawdown in support could open a security vacuum.

'REAL HOUSEWIVES' STAR LEAH MCSWEENEY PLANNING TO FLEE NYC OVER CRIME, CITY LEADERS WHO 'DO NOT CARE'

Seidemann recommended that if the judge does approve an overflow room, "it include only an audio feed so as to minimize the potential for witness intimidation and harassment."

World.title: Palantir's Shyam Sankar says ‘every day we’re making progress’ as AI supercharges American workers

WASHINGTON, D.C. — Palantir CTO Shyam Sankar said he’s seen significant progress since his Fox News op-ed imploring America to take advantage of both AI and the American worker, while sharing some observations on China’s use of AI.

"China treats AI as industrial policy," Sankar wrote on X in July. "Our labs treat it as theology, a race to birth a machine god. Beijing's play: commoditize the complement. All that frontier lab market cap gets transmuted into demand signal to scale the stack below the models: power, chips, minerals, etc. Americans can and must win the full stack."

Yet, Sankar acknowledged that even if America's not thinking about how to scale AI in all these other industries like China, it will happen naturally in the U.S. as the technology develops.

THE BIGGEST THREAT IN AMERICA'S RACE WITH CHINA ISN'T BEIJING, TECH EXECUTIVE WARNS

"The only threat to AI generating prosperity for America is suicide and homicide," Sankar told Fox News Digital at Palantir's American Builder Summit in July. "I'm not really worried about what is China going to do per se. I'm more worried about bans on data centers and kind of unfettered and unwarranted fears curtailing our ability to actually generate wage growth for the American worker."

"And so, I think really having a strong narrative that is told not by any companies, but actually by the people themselves is important for us to get excited and motivated and get lined up behind that opportunity," he added.

In February, Sankar wrote an op-ed for Fox News Digital noting that in order to catch up to China, the U.S. would have to harness the tools at its disposal: the American worker and AI.

"AI development and deployment should prioritize American workers and American industry," he wrote. "The goal is not efficiency in the abstract — it is American prosperity in the concrete."

PALANTIR'S SHYAM SANKAR: AMERICANS ARE ‘BEING LIED TO’ ABOUT AI JOB DISPLACEMENT FEARS

"China's manufacturing productivity grows at 6% per year. Ours grows at 0.4%. If we don't invest in AI and automation, we'll lose. The American worker with AI superpowers erodes China's competitive advantage."

Sankar believes the U.S. has made significant progress since the piece's publication.

"Yeah, I think every day we're making progress," Sankar told Fox News Digital. "I always love the — I have a very small submarine parts manufacturer, and it used to take them two weeks to do their production plan. During that period of time, the line was down, they weren't making any parts. So with AI, they've been able to take that down to less than an hour.

PALANTIR'S SHYAM SANKAR: US MUST USE AI AS ‘SLINGSHOT’ AGAINST CHINA OR FACE ECONOMIC DEFEAT

"So now they actually have more parts to make than they had people. They only had two shifts before, they hired a third shift," he continued. "There is no one on that shift who thinks, 'Hey, I got my job because of AI, but that's actually what happened. In a fundamentally supply-constrained economy, which we are, if you can get rid of the deadweight loss, you can unleash productivity. And I think every company is kind of leaning into and taking advantage of that."

Palantir's American Builders Summit in late July celebrated the efforts of their American Tech Fellowship grads. The alumni shared their stories and showed how they’re using AI to amplify their trade craft and advance their professions.

World.title: Country star Tyler Hubbard says ‘The Chosen’ brought the Bible to life for his family

Country singer, Tyler Hubbard, is sharing why his most recent musical project is special for him.

During a recent interview with Fox News Digital, the 39-year-old musician spoke about the upcoming season of "The Chosen" and his corresponding album, as well as how the television show brought the Bible alive for his children and has started a "lot of conversations about Jesus and about all the different stories of his life."

"We talk through all these stories, we talk through all their questions, but then it doesn't go in one ear and out the other," he said. "It really kind of sticks. It could be two years down the road, we'll be reading a Bible story and they'll already know it. They're kind of teaching us or teaching their friends at that point."

He called the idea that the show helps his kids understand the Bible better "a testimony to how well the show is produced and how accurate" the stories it is telling are, saying it "is really special" to reference them in the Bible and then "reliving it with the kids."

MORGAN WALLEN AND ELLA LANGLEY HOLD THE TOP TWO ALBUM SPOTS IN AMERICA FOR FIRST HALF OF 2026

Hubbard shared that he and his family watch the show together as a tradition, noting that "it's really opened up our kids' eyes to the gospel and to Jesus and how he lived." When the chance to write a song for the show came up, Hubbard admits he "was excited about the opportunity."

WATCH: Tyler Hubbard says 'The Chosen' brings stories from the bible alive for his kids

"It was just one of those things where a buddy of mine said, 'Hey, I've got the opportunity to letting us write a song for 'The Chosen' and if they like it, they might use it for something,' And I thought, 'Well, that'd be really cool.' Just something a little different for me," he said.

He explained that growing up he got into music by "leading worship in church," so "getting to write a faith-based song, a song that has some meat on the bone" and a deeper meaning, "and some heart and some truth behind it was really cool."

"So we had a great day and ended up that 'The Chosen' team really liked the song, and it turned into something special and something I'm proud of and excited to be a part of," he added.

The song, "All I Need Is You," is the first single from the new album inspired by the show, and will be featured on the soundtrack of its upcoming sixth season. It dropped on Aug. 7. The unnamed album, from 5&2 Studios and Capitol Christian Music Group, is set to debut in the fall.

He also spoke with Fox News Digital about a unique injury he had while on a recent fishing trip with his family.

WATCH: Tyler Hubbard was 'excited' to write a song for season six of 'The Chosen'

"I was just fishing one morning, and I was on a river bank and I got caught in a bush with my back cast and I went to cast it and it just, I had a treble hook just stick me pretty hard right in the back of the head. I ended up, I couldn't get it out myself," he shared.

TYLER HUBBARD STAYS CALM AS WIFE PULLS FISH HOOK FROM HIS SCALP ON FAMILY CAMPING VACATION

After trying and failing to get it out himself, he "asked for some help from my wife," who then "spent about a half an hour dealing with it." During that time, his son took his phone and began filming the removal process.

"And we did have some people be like, you should probably go, maybe get that checked out, or maybe have someone else take it out. But I was pretty determined. I was like, 'Baby, you got to get this hook out of here, cause I don't want to leave this place and I don't want to mess up this day.' So anyway, she did a good job."

In the background of the video, viewers can hear the couple's children asking various questions out of concern. One asks, "Is it bleeding mom?" with Tyler telling him, "Probably not bleeding a lot but it might be a little."

World.title: I watched Chicago promise food equity. Now my neighborhood has empty shelves
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

On the South Side of Chicago, we all know the script. The government announces with great fanfare some new program that is going to come save us and make our lives better. Ribbons are cut, and the aldermen and bureaucrats toast themselves as saviors, another notch of the "good" in their belts. Then time passes and, as sure as a 30-point game used to be for Michael Jordan, the program fails and there’s no one around to own up to the failure.

We recently experienced another failure when, on July 25, seven Save A Lot stores operated by Yellow Banana on Chicago’s South and West Sides closed their doors for good.

By closing day, shoppers encountered half-empty shelves and little fresh produce, tangible evidence that the stores were shutting down. Where can they go now in neighborhoods already struggling with limited options? My own immediate neighborhood doesn't have one supermarket. We have residents without cars and residents with disabilities, and they’re wondering where they can go next.

GOVERNMENT-RUN GROCERY STORES FACE RENEWED SCRUTINY AFTER CHICAGO'S EXPERIMENT FIZZLES

One local woman even stepped up and said she would love to take over the Englewood store at 63rd and Halsted and make it work for the community where she grew up. They didn’t listen to her or care. The store still closed.

Beginning under Mayor Lori Lightfoot, Chicago committed millions in public financing to rehabilitate and reopen six Save A Lot stores on the South and West Sides as part of an effort to preserve grocery access.

Many of us saw the problem right off the bat: the government was funding both the stores (the supply side) and the customers (the demand side). Chicago provided Yellow Banana with $13.5 million in TIF financing to acquire, rehabilitate and reopen six Save A Lot locations.

Taxpayers were supporting both sides of the equation: Chicago subsidized the stores' redevelopment, while many shoppers relied on federally funded SNAP benefits to buy groceries.

EXPERTS SCORCH MAMDANI'S GROCERY PLAN AS AN 'ILLUSION' THAT WILL HAVE TAXPAYERS FOOTING THE BILL

At the same time, many customers relied on federally funded SNAP benefits to purchase food.

Save A Lot said the stores had experienced a 26% year-over-year decline in SNAP/EBT tender types and cited reductions in SNAP benefits as one of the financial pressures on the stores.

When the SNAP benefits were cut, the stores saw a sharp drop in SNAP/EBT transactions.

To me, that illustrates the vulnerability of government-supported retail models when their economics depend heavily on continued public assistance.

When the survival of a store rests on government money flowing to both the seller and the buyer, you do not have a market. You have a political arrangement that is only as stable as the next appropriation. Cut either subsidy and the shelves empty out.

It was Chicago Mayor Brandon Johnson who took many of us White-guilt Chicagoans on this "grand" vision. When he first announced that he was exploring the idea of government grocery stores, he said: "All Chicagoans deserve to live near convenient, affordable, healthy grocery options. We know access to grocery stores is already a challenge for many residents, especially on the South and West Sides."

He promised the people the golden road to food equity.

Johnson's proposal was separate from the Lightfoot-era Yellow Banana deal, but it reflected the same instinct: when private grocery access falls short, turn to government intervention. The collapse of the Yellow Banana arrangement should give Chicagoans every reason to be skeptical of that approach.

GROCER-TURNED-LAWMAKER SAYS MAMDANI’S GOVERNMENT-RUN STORES 'MIGHT NOT EVEN LAST A YEAR’

Look at the results of government-backed efforts in those same neighborhoods: closed stores and empty shelves. The mayor and his administration are now arranging transportation assistance for some affected seniors—another government response to a problem government spending failed to solve.

This same idiocy is repeating itself in New York City, where Mayor Zohran Mamdani is creating government-owned grocery stores.

New York has allocated $70 million for five planned municipal grocery stores, while the projected cost associated with constructing the planned 9,000-square-foot La Marqueta location has been reported at roughly $30 million.

I wonder if a real entrepreneur could launch a better-run store for just $4 to $5 million? But who knows? The socialist always responds to failure with the statement that true socialism has yet to be tried.

MY WALK ACROSS AMERICA IS OVER, BUT MY MISSION FOR SOUTH SIDE KIDS IS NOT

The notion that government can do it better than the private citizen is absolute nonsense. Private owners succeed or fail by serving customers well, and this means quality, selection, prices and cleanliness. The government does not know that business. A bureaucrat is not a businessman. Bureaucrats playing with other people’s money have no skin in the game, and that means waste, inefficiency and, ultimately, failure. And the very people they tooted their horns about helping are now worse off.

Thomas Sowell said, "Although the big word on the left is ‘compassion,’ the big agenda on the left is dependency."

Shelby Steele later added that by accepting the idea that government will take over the responsibility that only we can take, "we relinquished authority over ourselves. We became child-like."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

What no one is saying is how the government has played a huge role in creating the conditions for these food deserts in the first place. It has cut off pathways to opportunity or incentivized people to stay dependent. Failing schools. Violent, unsafe streets that drive businesses away. Rules and policies that punish work and reward staying stuck in intergenerational poverty. A culture of dependency that tells people they are permanent victims who need the state as a caretaker. This is what they call the permanent underclass.

Now, the same government that helped create the problem wants to ride in as the savior, promising that its sterile, taxpayer-funded grocery stores will fix everything?

Our people want good schools with great teachers, safe playgrounds, paved roads, local businesses that can actually open and thrive, loans for homes and small enterprises, and real pathways to opportunity. We pay taxes. Government has a responsibility to provide the most basic elements of civic viability, and this means law and order, safety, parks and basic functioning services. Yet these neighborhoods are now also saddled with empty supermarkets, adding to an already blighted landscape.

Our people have been told America is evil, so government must ride to the rescue. They’ve been told the rich are out to get them, so government must redistribute. They’ve been fed nothing but hate for this country. But America is not a failure. We forget that America is an idea, a set of principles: individual liberty, personal responsibility, and the right to rise by your own effort. Principles are just principles, and they cannot fail. It is the people who abandon those principles who fail.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

What happened in Chicago is a warning. We know that Mamdani and his supporters in New York are too arrogant to listen, and those stores will fail or sink into mediocrity with time. Where will Mamdani be then?

The people of Chicago, New York, and communities all across our country should demand something better. They should push for the principles that made America work in the first place.

World.title: Arizona Gov. Katie Hobbs chooses former Republican as running mate in re-election bid
World.content:
Arizona’s Democratic Gov. Katie Hobbs has chosen a former Republican as her running mate for her re-election bid this November.

On Tuesday, Hobbs named John Giles, who served as a GOP mayor of Mesa, Arizona, from 2014 to 2025, as her pick for lieutenant governor.

In a joint video announcement with Giles, Hobbs said she has fought for Arizonans as governor by cutting taxes, securing the border and supporting public safety.

“Now, for the first time in our state’s history, we are electing a governor and lieutenant governor on the same ticket. And the first thing I looked for in a running mate was someone who shares that value of putting Arizonans ahead of partisan politics,” Hobbs said.

Giles said, “I was a lifelong Republican before becoming an independent because extremists shouldn’t stand in the way of getting things done.”

Giles changed his party affiliation to independent in May and voted in the Democratic primary last month, Hobbs’ communications director Michael Beyer confirmed to NBC News.

Voters will elect a lieutenant governor for the first time this fall after a ballot measure creating the position was approved in the 2022 election.

The New York Times was first to report on Hobbs’ plans.

Hobbs faces a competitive race against Rep. Andy Biggs, R-Ariz., who previously chaired the conservative House Freedom Caucus and has served in Congress since 2017. Biggs has selected former state lawmaker Sine Kerr as his running mate. Biggs won the Republican primary last month, beating fellow Rep. David Schweikert and businessmen Scott Neely and Ken Miceli.

While mayor of Mesa, Giles endorsed then-Vice President Kamala Harris for president in the 2024 election and spoke at the Democratic National Convention in Chicago that year about his disappointment with the Republican Party.

“I’m a lifelong Republican, so I feel a little out of place tonight. But I feel more at home here than in today’s Republican Party,” Giles said in his remarks. “The Grand Old Party has been kidnapped by extremists and devolved into a cult — the cult of Donald Trump.”

He added, “I have an urgent message for the majority of Americans who, like me, are in the political middle. John McCain’s Republican Party is gone, and we don’t owe a damn thing to what’s been left behind.”

The nonpartisan Cook Political Report rated the governor’s race as leaning Democratic in the battleground state, which President Donald Trump carried in 2016 and 2024 and Joe Biden won in 2020.

In 2022, Hobbs defeated Republican Kari Lake in the gubernatorial election by less than 1 percentage point. Before serving as governor, Hobbs was Arizona’s secretary of state and was also the minority leader in the state Senate and a member of the state House.

Hobbs recently formed a coalition of former and current Republican and independent leaders who support her re-election, which included Giles and more than 50 other business leaders and officials.

The Democratic incumbent has touted her record of working across the aisle, including signing more than 900 pieces of bipartisan legislation into law, according to her campaign. She has also highlighted her efforts to expand affordable housing, secure the border and her repeal of the state’s 1864 total abortion ban

Biggs, meanwhile, has promoted his relationship with Trump and has run on a campaign touting his support for lowering taxes and border security.

World.title: Lauren Boebert’s 21-year-old son is arrested on child sexual exploitation charges
World.content:
The son of Rep. Lauren Boebert, R-Colo., was arrested on charges of sexual exploitation of a child, authorities said Monday.

Tyler Boebert, 21, was taken into custody Sunday and later released on $10,000 bond, the Garfield County Sheriff’s Office said in a statement.

Tyler Boebert did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

“I love my son,” Lauren Boebert said in a statement Monday. “We take allegations very seriously and pray for everyone affected during this challenging time.”

It was not immediately clear whether Tyler Boebert has a lawyer to speak on his behalf. An attorney who previously represented him in a separate case did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The charges are linked to a 2024 video Tyler Boebert allegedly recorded with a 17-year-old, according to an affidavit in support of an arrest warrant. He was 18 at the time.

The 17-year-old’s mother later alerted authorities that a video showing her daughter and Tyler Boebert having sex was posted on Instagram, the affidavit says. The affidavit does not say who is alleged to have posted the video.

Tyler Boebert was charged with three counts of sexual exploitation of a child and two counts of contributing to the delinquency of a minor, court records show.

He was previously arrested on charges police described as a string of vehicle trespass and property thefts.

That case continues, according to Colorado Public Radio.

After her son was arrested in 2024, Lauren Boebert said he had been through “some very difficult, public challenges for a young man and the subject of attention that he didn’t ask for.”

“It breaks my heart to see my child struggling and, in this situation, especially when he has been provided multiple opportunities to get his life on track,” she said. “I will never give up on him, and I will continue to be there for him.”

World.title: Luigi Mangione returns to court less than a month before state trial
World.content:
Luigi Mangione appeared in a New York courtroom Tuesday for what could be the final hearing before his state murder trial begins next month.

Mangione, 28, has pleaded not guilty to several state charges in connection with the December 2024 fatal shooting of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson outside the New York Hilton Midtown.

At Tuesday’s hearing, New York Supreme Court Justice Gregory Carro is expected to determine jury selection logistics — a task that could prove challenging given the case’s notoriety. Jury selection is set to begin Sept. 8.

If convicted, Mangione faces up to life in prison.

On Tuesday, the courtroom was filled with journalists and some Mangione proponents, who were wearing green, a color that appeared to reference the Luigi character from the iconic Nintendo Super Mario games and subsequent movies.

Mangione entered the courtroom from a holding area wearing a gray suit. He glanced around the room before taking his seat next to his attorneys Karen Friedman Agnifilo, Marc Agnifilo and Jacob Kaplan.

Justice Gregory Carro ruled at the start of the hearing that the jury would be anonymous, a designation that is becoming increasingly more common in high-profile court cases in New York.

Carro also said there would be expanded press and public access to the trial. After fielding complaints from Mangione’s defense team about potential space limitations, court administrators arranged for an overflow room.

“It has always been under consideration, they had to find the physical place and it had to be staffed,” Carro said.

Mangione’s case has garnered international headlines, with mostly female supporters who have appeared in court throughout the pretrial hearings and argue that his actions were justified.

Prosecutors allege Mangione was motivated by an animus toward the health insurance industry, but he was never a UnitedHealthcare customer. He had no connection to Thompson, a father of two from Minnesota.

Mangione allegedly trailed Thompson and identified his movements in New York, where the prominent health care executive was attending his company’s investors conference, prosecutors say.

He then allegedly shot Thompson from behind outside the hotel, then fled the city. He was apprehended several days later in Altoona, Pa., after a McDonald’s employee called the police.

Former Manhattan prosecutor Rebecca Roiphe told NBC News that during jury selection, prosecutors will likely want to scrutinize potential jurors’ experiences in the health care system to weed out those who might sympathize with Mangione.

“I think the prosecution is clearly going to want to keep off people who have some kind of axe to grind about health care,” Roiphe said.

Roiphe, who is now a criminal law and ethics professor at New York Law School, believes the defense will seek panelists with a “healthcare for all mindset.”

Mangione separately faces federal stalking-related charges in New York and has pleaded not guilty. The Justice Department was seeking the death penalty in the federal case, but that option was taken off the table earlier this year.

U.S. District Judge Margaret Garnett issued a ruling in January that effectively blocks New York federal prosecutors from pursuing a capital case.

World.title: Perseid meteor shower reaches peak viewing on Wednesday night
World.content:
The Perseid meteor shower is set to provide a late-summer show in the skies over the United States.

The meteor shower, which NASA calls the best of the year, is set to peak on Aug. 12 and 13.

"With swift and bright meteors, Perseids frequently leave long 'wakes' of light and color behind them as they streak through Earth's atmosphere," according to NASA. "The Perseids are one of the most plentiful showers with about 50 to 100 meteors seen per hour."

For those who are trying to see the meteor shower on Wednesday night, the best time for viewing in the Northern Hemisphere is during the predawn hours on Aug. 13, but if you don't want to get up very early, you can still see them as early as 10 p.m. the night before.

Random meteors are visible in dark skies on any given night. Meteor showers tend to put on dazzling celestial shows and happen at predictable times every year when the Earth plows through trails of debris left behind by comets and, sometimes, asteroids. Those remnants collide with Earth's atmosphere at extremely high speeds, producing streaks of light known as shooting stars.

The Perseids are debris from comet 109P/Swift-Tuttle, an icy ball that orbits the sun every 133 years and isn't scheduled for a return visit until 2125. Observations of this meteor shower date back over 2,000 years.

The Perseids are a perennial favorite because they tend to produce brilliant fireballs. Summer temperatures also make this shower popular.

"We don't have to suffer through a cold winter night to get a good view of meteors," said astronomer Zach Vanderbosch with McDonald Observatory in Texas.

The moon will be in its new moon phase during the Perseids' peak, making viewing conditions even better.

"The moon is beautiful, but it's such a diva," said astronomer Aparna Venkatesan with the University of San Francisco. "New moon means we don't have moonlight flooding the sky, and you tend to see way more meteors as a result."

To spot the meteors, go outside after dark, away from clouds and city lights. Venkatesan plans to drive to the Sierra Nevada.

The best views will be between midnight and dawn when the constellation Perseus is high in the northern sky. The meteors will appear to radiate from that constellation.

Look up and give your eyes a half hour to adjust to the darkness. Vanderbosch recommends picking a patch of sky to focus on until a quick, bright streak passes by — even in your peripheral vision — and to avoid looking at your phone.

"There's just something magical about it," Vanderbosch said.

World.title: 1 year in, National Guard became a part of D.C. life. And, deadly quake hits Colombia
World.content:
1 year in, National Guard became a part of D.C. life. And, deadly quake hits Colombia

Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

Today's top stories

Today marks a year since thousands of National Guard members began patrolling the streets of Washington, D.C., as part of the Trump administration's anti-crime mission. The armed troops' presence in the nation's capital has since been quietly extended to Inauguration Day 2029, marking the longest and largest National Guard deployment under this administration. President Trump ordered the deployment in the nation's capital last year after declaring a "crime emergency" and launching the D.C. Safe and Beautiful Task Force, despite violent crime being at a 30-year low. The nonpartisan watchdog Project on Government Oversight estimates that this deployment will cost around $3 billion by 2029, and multiple studies have since found that the National Guard's presence has had no effect on violent crime.

toggle caption Kent Nishimura/AFP via Getty Images

Six states hold primary elections today. In parts of Alabama, some residents are voting for a second time this primary season, after newly redrawn congressional maps pushed the primaries for some districts from May to August. The changes have some residents worried that confusion could affect voter turnout. In the Midwest, Minnesota and Wisconsin's primaries will test the power of progressive candidates against more traditional Democrats, one week after Abdul El-Sayed narrowly defeated the more moderate Rep. Haley Stevens in Michigan. Several Trump-endorsed candidates are on the ballot in key races, including MyPillow founder Mike Lindell for governor of Minnesota. The president is also supporting the late Sen. Lindsey Graham's sister, Darline Graham, for the Senate in South Carolina.

Sponsor Message

More than 130 people have died after a powerful 7.4 magnitude earthquake in western Colombia caused extensive destruction yesterday. Authorities report that the death toll is expected to rise as search and rescue efforts continue.



🎧 The damage is affecting four cities and many smaller towns along western Colombia, according to reporter Manuel Rueda. Cali, Pereira, Manizales and Quibdo have been hit the hardest. The area spans around 250 miles top to bottom across the country. Rueda says rescue teams could struggle to reach remote regions like Choco due to poor road conditions and limited airports. Many survivors have chosen to sleep outside to avoid the risk of further collapses, and some are seeking shelter in places like stadiums.

Trump signed an executive order yesterday to change childhood vaccination requirements for dangerous infectious diseases. The order calls for reducing the number of federally recommended vaccines from 17 to 11 and splitting up the MMR shot for measles, mumps and rubella. Trump's action seeks to accomplish goals similar to those set by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention in January, which a judge later blocked. The new order is also likely to face legal challenges.

Deep dive

Demand for testosterone is surging, driven by social media trends like "T-maxxing," online direct-to-consumer clinics and high-profile figures like podcaster Joe Rogan. The U.S. military is even planning to test service members for low levels of the hormone. The Food and Drug Administration has signaled that it wants to revise its criteria to make testosterone therapy accessible for men with low levels regardless of underlying cause, if low libido is a symptom. Here's a breakdown of the debate around testosterone and its safety:

Sponsor Message

➡️ In the early 2000s, testosterone was a rapidly growing prescription drug in the United States. After studies suggested it increased heart attack and stroke risks, the FDA issued warnings and mandated a safety study.

➡️ The trial published in 2023 found no increased risk of heart attack, stroke or major cardiovascular events compared to placebo, though it did raise other concerns, like higher risk of fractures. These findings led the FDA to remove the cardiovascular risk warning language from the products.

➡️ Dr. Steven Woloshin, who has testified against a drug company that makes testosterone, argues that removing the language was premature due to major limitations in the study. These include an insufficient follow-up period to assess potential harms, and that testosterone levels in the blood were not raised to typical clinical practice levels.

Cameroonian painter Marc Padeu is reimagining classical Western paintings by infusing them with inspiration from his hometown. His works take images often seen as belonging exclusively to Europe — such as the Nativity and the Last Supper — and make Black figures and African culture focal points. He says his goal isn't to rewrite history, but to explore the universal themes in these images: birth, death, sacrifice, promise and hope. Padeu points out that many religious scenes feature ordinary people like fishermen, shepherds and craftsmen, which makes it natural to bring these stories back to life with the men and women who work the land today. His art is now featured in a new London gallery show, but you don't have to visit to get a peek. See the vibrant photos from Padeu's collection.
