My parents took a big risk when they moved their newborn twins from Manhattan to a small town in central Mexico. Yet, I couldn’t be more grateful that they did.

My family came to San Miguel de Allende when I was six months old, and I lived there until I was 15. And although we love San Miguel, my parents thought it best to send me back to the United States for high school. Having mastered the arts of reading, writing and calculating in Mexican schools, I think it’s safe to say that I learned to be a student there.

I attended SMA-based Academia Internacional from preschool through third grade. Their school emphasizes diversity and individuality, with a multicultural student body comprising both Mexican and American students. At Academia, I met my best friends and made my favorite childhood memories. I began studying French in the third grade, took advanced English classes through the Cambridge program at school, performed dance shows at the local theater and, most importantly, became queen of the monkey bars.

In fourth grade, I transferred to Colegio Newland, another bilingual and diverse school that emphasizes leadership and hands-on learning. The school follows an innovative curriculum that integrates technology into the classroom, with much of our learning centered around a platform called Knotion. At Newland, I was the middle school student body president, competed in spelling bees, traveled to geography competitions in other cities and even created a haircare brand for my entrepreneurship class. I also played tennis and took piano lessons outside of school.

As I reflect on my schooling, I realize many people assume the Mexican education system is mediocre or easy. But in reality, it challenged me while providing a foundation I needed to comfortably transition to a U.S. high school. I recall my middle school teachers constantly assigning pop quizzes, and to make matters worse, they would hand back our tests from lowest grade to highest — yikes. I struggled a lot in the subject of history, and after failing an exam, I spent weeks studying to improve my grade, only to discover that the content was fascinating. Thanks to Newland, I found a passion for it.

My parents loved raising my brother and me in San Miguel and considered it the perfect place for young children. However, they believed it made sense for us to return to the United States for high school. And like many parents, mine worried about the transition and whether I was academically prepared for a more “rigorous” school. Nevertheless, they were confident my brother and I would be okay because of the values we grew up learning. In San Miguel, people respect each other, always offer help and love to joke around. My brother and I were raised with those same values. And because of them, we adapted and made friends quickly.

I started by studying for the SSAT, the entrance exam required by most private high schools in the U.S., and it was rough. In Mexico, standardized tests barely exist, so I was unfamiliar with the idea of them. Additionally, I had never taken an exam in English, making it difficult to understand academic vocabulary. However, being fluent in Spanish often helped me identify the meaning of words with Latin roots. And ironically, my Mexican upbringing was the strongest part of my application as I drew on my childhood experiences in my essays. I wrote about Christmas, listening to mariachis and visiting Oaxaca.

After a long admissions process, I enrolled in a small boarding school in northern California. At first, the Spanish-to-English transition was difficult. My first year, I remember getting a 60% on a physics exam and feeling completely defeated. But seeing my international friends excel after going through the same transition motivated me to keep trying my best.

It’s crazy to think that I moved away from home at just 15. My parents still live in Mexico while I’m at school thousands of miles away. Of course I was scared to be on my own, but growing up between two cultures has made adapting to a new environment much easier, and California has quickly become my second home.

Throughout the two years that I’ve studied in the U.S., I’ve learned so much. My love for history persists and I have even grown to like math! (sort of). I found that attending Spanish-speaking schools didn’t hold me back, but rather, it is one of the most fascinating parts of who I am.

Now, I am going into my senior year, in which I will be editor-in-chief of the school newspaper and a prefect in the dorms. I continue to challenge myself academically with Advanced Placement (AP) and Honors courses, and can’t wait to have as much fun as possible with my friends.

As the college application process begins, I continue to write about my Mexican upbringing in every essay. I couldn’t be more grateful to have grown up and studied in such a beautiful place. I truly believe that I wouldn’t be as outgoing, determined or academically accomplished had my parents chosen to raise me in Manhattan instead.

Zella Golden grew up in San Miguel de Allende and is a senior in high school in Marin, California. Golden is completing an internship with MND.

World.title: Taylor Farms recalls its Mexico-sourced jalapeños, cuts ties with Sinaloa supplier over salmonella scare
World.content:
Just weeks after Taylor Farms voluntarily recalled iceberg lettuce products sourced from central Mexico, the Salinas, California-based company is voluntarily recalling some products that include jalapeño chiles due to concerns about possible salmonella contamination.

The decision by Taylor Fresh Foods — the parent company — is linked to a recall issued by San Diego-based Coast Citrus Distributors, which announced it was voluntarily recalling fresh jalapeños due to food safety concerns.

Taylor Fresh Foods said in a statement that it is not aware of any reported illnesses linked to its products containing jalapeños.

In its own statement, Coast Citrus said it will “no longer” source peppers from a farmer based in the northwestern Mexican state of Sinaloa, while it “seeks alternative suppliers.”

Taylor Fresh Foods also stated that it no longer purchases products from the Sinaloa farmer and “will fulfill orders with alternative suppliers.”

Besides the chiles themselves, guacamole, pico de gallo, taco salsa, burritos and spicy sandwiches are among the jalapeño-containing prepared foods included in the latest Taylor Farms recall.

Several U.S. states have been notified that all such products that feature a “Best If Used By” date up to and including Aug. 16, 2026, have been recalled. The products were sold at stores such as Kroger, Stop & Shop, Target, Whole Foods, Trader Joe’s and Walmart.

The recall comes as a result of a salmonella outbreak in the U.S. linked to jalapeño peppers imported from Mexico that had sickened 345 people in 27 states and led to 36 hospitalizations as of last Wednesday.

The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) issued an alert on Aug. 5, while the Food and Drug Administration is “working to determine if recalled jalapeños went to grocery stores,” so additional recalls could be announced.

As a result of the alert, Coast Citrus immediately agreed to recall the affected products and notify its customers. The Chipotle Mexican Grill and Qdoba restaurant chains also stopped serving the jalapeños in question.

Salmonella infections can cause diarrhea, fever and stomach cramps, and can be especially serious in young children, the elderly and people with weakened immune systems. The illness usually lasts four to seven days, and most people recover without treatment.

The latest recall comes amid heightened scrutiny of food safety in the U.S. restaurant industry, following last month’s outbreak of cyclosporiasis — a parasitic disease — linked to iceberg lettuce served at Taco Bell restaurants that was reportedly sourced from central Mexico.

With reports from RTV Noticias, The Associated Press, the BBC and La Jornada

World.title: MND Local: Why is Puerto Vallarta so quiet right now?
World.content:
Walk around Puerto Vallarta right now and something feels different.

It’s not simply quieter in the way Vallarta is meant to feel during low season. There aren’t just shorter waits at restaurants, and there isn’t just a little more room on the beach.

It’s empty.

Restaurants have tables sitting unused. Tour operators are seeing smaller groups. Businesses that depend on visitors are wondering when the crowds will return.

More than just the ‘low season’

Anyone who has lived here for a while knows that summer is slower. That’s nothing new. But this one? This one feels different.

And the question being asked across the city is simple: “Where did everybody go?”

The events of Feb. 22 certainly didn’t help. The violence that followed the military operation against cartel leader Nemesio Oseguera Cervantes, known as El Mencho, brought roadblocks, burned vehicles, disruptions and international headlines. Several airlines temporarily suspended flights to Puerto Vallarta as the situation unfolded.

For those here at the time, the reality was more complicated than the images broadcast around the world. The immediate crisis passed quickly, and Puerto Vallarta reopened even faster.

But for people watching those images thousands of kilometers away, they may have been all they saw. Fear has a far longer memory than a roadblock.

A viewer in Canada or the United States doesn’t necessarily distinguish between what happened that day and what Puerto Vallarta was like the day after, let alone what it’s like six months later.

If your only knowledge of a place comes from television footage showing burning vehicles and blocked roads, you might think twice about booking a holiday there, too.

However, February isn’t the whole story.

Increased competition for travelers

Travelers have more choices now, and Puerto Vallarta is competing harder for holiday dollars. Airfares and promotions matter, and more destinations are competing for the same travelers than ever before.

People can visit somewhere new, find a cheaper flight, take advantage of a resort promotion elsewhere or simply decide after several trips to Vallarta that they would like a change of scenery.

For a family deciding where to spend a week, a few hundred dollars makes a big difference.

Travelers don’t owe Puerto Vallarta their vacation, which means the city has to keep earning their business. That includes offering solid value.

Some may point out the prices certain restaurants are charging right now.

There are places in Puerto Vallarta where prices have climbed to the point that visitors can legitimately ask whether the experience still represents good value for money, particularly when compared with other destinations.

Yet there is another side to that conversation.

The economics of tourism

Restaurant owners still have employees to pay. They have rent, electricity, ingredients, maintenance, taxes and a list of other costs that don’t disappear because it’s August and the tables are empty.

When fewer people come through the door, every customer matters more. That doesn’t make every price reasonable, nor does it mean visitors should simply pay whatever they are asked. But to encourage lower prices, businesses need both a reason and a way to reduce them.

Volume matters. A restaurant with full tables can afford to make a little less per customer. A tour operator with full boats can offer a better deal. A shop with steady foot traffic can move more product at a smaller margin.

When the customers aren’t there, the math changes. That’s where the impact of a quiet tourism season spreads far beyond the hotel lobby.

Tourism isn’t just hotels. It’s the taxi driver waiting for a fare. It’s the server whose income depends partly on tips. The boat captain. The tour guide. The massage therapist. The shop owner. The market vendor. The person cleaning vacation rentals. It’s an enormous economic ecosystem that most people don’t consider until something goes wrong.

Why locals matter

The question isn’t necessarily whether businesses have any customers. It’s whether they have enough to make the numbers work. That’s where full-time residents come in, because local residents have far more influence than they realize.

Foreign residents often fall into the trap of thinking, “I’m not a tourist. Tourism doesn’t really affect me.”

It does. Local restaurants employ neighbors. Local shops generate community income. Taxis, tours and business recommendations all drive the surrounding economy.

One response to a quiet summer is surprisingly simple: Go out.

Try the restaurant you’ve been meaning to visit. Use the independent shop with the quirky knickknack that caught your eye. Book the local tour you’ve thought about taking. Catch a bus and venture beyond the tourist zone.

Leave a review. Recommend a business. Spend money locally. And when someone back home asks whether Puerto Vallarta is still worth visiting, tell the truth.

A shared investment

Yes, there was violence on Feb. 22. Yes, Vallarta deals with crime, traffic, construction and infrastructure issues. But it also offers extraordinary natural beauty, remarkable food, generous people, neighborhoods full of character and a community that continues to evolve.

Both things can be true.

Don’t sell a fantasy. Tell people why you still live here. Long-term residents offer something tourism campaigns never will: personal credibility.

When a government campaign says Puerto Vallarta is wonderful, people expect it — it’s a sales pitch. But when someone who has lived here for five, 10 or 20 years says, “I know the problems. I know what happened. And I still think you should come,” that carries real weight.

Maybe this unusually quiet summer is a warning. Maybe it’s simply a blip. Either way, it would be foolish not to pay attention.

The question shouldn’t only be “Where did everybody go?” It should also be “What can residents do to make sure they want to come back?” That starts with remembering that tourism isn’t an entitlement; it’s an investment everyone shares.

When those tables sit empty, the impact doesn’t stop with the restaurant owner. It ripples out, eventually reaching everyone who calls Puerto Vallarta home.

And when home is hurting, no one is untouched.

Charlotte Smith is a writer and journalist based in Mexico. Her work focuses on travel, politics and community. You can follow along with her travel stories at www.salsaandserendipity.com.

World.title: Latin America Needs Four Workers to Match One American, IDB Finds
World.content:
Latin America · Economy

Key Facts Productivity ratio Latin America’s labour productivity is about 26% of the US level, requiring nearly four regional workers to match one US worker.

Latin America’s labour productivity is about 26% of the US level, requiring nearly four regional workers to match one US worker. Formality rate Only 46% of workers in the region hold formal jobs with social-security coverage.

Only 46% of workers in the region hold formal jobs with social-security coverage. Slow progress Informality fell by just eight percentage points over two decades.

Informality fell by just eight percentage points over two decades. Skills gap More than 40% of workers lack the basic literacy and numeracy skills required for their jobs.

More than 40% of workers lack the basic literacy and numeracy skills required for their jobs. Structural causes Low investment in physical and technological capital, weak innovation, and human-capital gaps underpin the shortfall.

Low investment in physical and technological capital, weak innovation, and human-capital gaps underpin the shortfall. Policy fixes The IDB recommends vocational training, stronger social protection, formal hiring incentives, and regulatory reform.

A new IDB report quantifies the region’s deep productivity deficit and points to informality, skills mismatches, and weak investment as the core obstacles.

For anyone following Latin America’s economic trajectory, the latest Inter-American Development Bank (IDB) report delivers a sobering benchmark: Latin America’s productivity gap means the region needs almost four workers to produce what one US worker does, a structural drag that explains stagnant wages, fragile social safety nets, and persistent inequality across the region.

A street market in Zacatlán, Puebla, Mexico. (Photo: Adam Jones, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

The scale of the gap

The IDB’s study, titled “Hacer que los mercados laborales funcionen” (“Making Labor Markets Work”), puts Latin America’s labour productivity at roughly 26% of the US level. That is not a cyclical dip but a long-run equilibrium shaped by decades of underinvestment and weak institutional incentives. The report, released in August 2026, frames this as a failure of labour markets to allocate talent and capital efficiently, with consequences for both output and worker well-being.

The gap is not uniform across sectors, but the aggregate figure is stark. It implies that a typical Latin American worker produces little more than a quarter of their US counterpart’s output. This disparity helps explain why the region’s middle classes remain vulnerable to shocks and why poverty reduction has slowed in recent years. The IDB stresses that closing even part of this gap would have outsized effects on living standards, but the path requires confronting uncomfortable structural realities.

Causes: informality, skills, and investment

The report identifies several interlocking causes. Chief among them is labour informality: only 46% of workers in Latin America and the Caribbean have formal jobs with social-security coverage. That means more than half of the workforce operates outside the protections and productivity-enhancing mechanisms of the formal economy, such as training, credit access, and legal recourse. The IDB notes that informality fell by only eight percentage points over 20 years, a glacial pace that suggests policy inertia rather than market forces.

Compounding this is a severe skills mismatch. The report finds that more than 40% of workers lack the basic literacy and numeracy skills needed for their jobs. This is not a fringe problem; it affects a large share of the employed population, limiting their ability to adopt new technologies or move into higher-value roles. On the investment side, the IDB points to chronically low spending on physical and technological capital, alongside weak innovation and an inefficient business environment marked by regulatory barriers, infrastructure deficiencies, and legal uncertainty. These factors discourage firms from upgrading equipment or expanding, trapping productivity at low levels.

What the IDB recommends

The IDB’s prescription is broad but concrete. It calls for expanding vocational and professional training programmes to close the skills gap, with a particular focus on workers already in the labour force rather than only new entrants. Strengthening social protection and pension systems is also central, but the bank is careful to link this to formalisation: benefits should be less dependent on job status, making formal hiring more attractive to both employers and workers.

Regulatory reform is the third pillar. The report argues that current rules often penalise formal employment, pushing firms and workers into informality. Simplifying registration, reducing red tape, and ensuring legal certainty for investors would help. The IDB also stresses that training and social protection should be designed to support labour mobility, allowing workers to move from informal to formal sectors without losing access to benefits. These measures, the bank argues, would raise productivity and well-being simultaneously, rather than trading one for the other.

The political economy of reform

None of these recommendations is new, but the IDB’s framing sharpens the urgency. The report implicitly acknowledges that previous reform efforts have failed because they were piecemeal or faced strong resistance from entrenched interests. Informality is not just a labour-market outcome; it is a political equilibrium in which many actors benefit from the status quo, including some workers who fear losing flexibility and some firms that avoid taxes and regulations.

The IDB’s emphasis on making benefits less dependent on job status is a subtle but important shift. It suggests a model where social protection follows the worker, not the contract, which could reduce the stigma and risk associated with formalisation. Whether governments in the region have the political capital to pursue such reforms remains an open question, but the report provides a clear evidence base for those who do. For now, the numbers speak for themselves: Latin America’s productivity gap is not inevitable, but closing it will require sustained, coordinated effort across multiple fronts.

Frequently Asked Questions

What exactly is labour productivity, and why does it matter? Labour productivity measures output per worker or worked. It matters because it determines wages, living standards, and a country’s ability to fund public services. Low productivity means workers produce less, earn less, and have fewer resources for education, health, and infrastructure. Is the 26% figure a recent development? No. The IDB report presents it as a long-standing structural feature, not a recent decline. The region has trailed US productivity for decades, and the gap has not narrowed significantly despite periods of economic growth. The report’s contribution is to quantify the gap and link it to specific policy failures. Can vocational training alone close the gap? No. Training is necessary but not sufficient. The IDB stresses that training must be paired with formalisation incentives, social-protection reforms, and regulatory changes. Without those complementary measures, workers may gain skills but remain in informal jobs where those skills are underused, limiting the impact on aggregate productivity.

Sources: Inter-American Development Bank (IDB); Forbes Colombia; El Colombiano; Revista Mercado.

World.title: Chile Wants Its Own Instant Payments — but Not a Central-Bank Pix
World.content:
Chile · Fintech

Key Facts Project name The private-bank-led instant payment rail is internally called ‘Tiro’.

The private-bank-led instant payment rail is internally called ‘Tiro’. Public milestone On Aug 5, 2026, the Banco Central de Chile said it would open a public consultation on rules for an instant payment system (SPI), expected in the third quarter.

On Aug 5, 2026, the Banco Central de Chile said it would open a public consultation on rules for an instant payment system (SPI), expected in the third quarter. Governance model Unlike Brazil’s Pix, Chile’s central bank will not build the rail itself; banks lead with BancoEstado participating.

Unlike Brazil’s Pix, Chile’s central bank will not build the rail itself; banks lead with BancoEstado participating. Third attempt Tiro follows earlier failed efforts, Paga2 and RedPay.

Tiro follows earlier failed efforts, Paga2 and RedPay. Core features The design includes alias-based transfers, QR codes, and use of the existing TEF network.

The design includes alias-based transfers, QR codes, and use of the existing TEF network. Timeline No launch is expected in the next few months; implementation timing remains uncertain.

Chile’s banks are building their own instant payment rail, but the central bank is setting the rules — and the project is still far from launch.

For anyone tracking Latin America’s payments landscape, the question is no longer whether Chile will get instant payments, but who will control the rails — and when they will actually arrive. The answer, based on the latest regulatory and industry signals, is that instant payments in Chile are coming, but not soon, and not in the way Brazil did it.

Illustrative: a contactless payment. (Photo: ING Nederland, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

What ‘Tiro’ Actually Is

The project internally named ‘Tiro’ is a proposed real-time payment system for account-to-account transfers between people and merchants. It is being led by private banks, with state-owned BancoEstado also at the table. The design under discussion includes alias-based payments, QR codes, and other identifiers, aiming to make transfers as simple as selecting a contact or scanning a code.

Rather than building new infrastructure from scratch, the banks plan to leverage Chile’s existing TEF transfer network as the technical base. That means the system could be layered onto current rails, potentially reducing costs and deployment time. But this is the third attempt at such a system in Chile: earlier projects, Paga2 and RedPay, failed to gain traction. Tiro is being treated with caution by industry observers, precisely because of that history.

The Pix Comparison & the Governance Debate

The most obvious reference point is Brazil’s Pix, which was built and operated by the central bank and became a mass-market phenomenon. Chile’s approach is fundamentally different: the Banco Central de Chile has explicitly ruled out building the rail itself, leaving the challenge to private actors. That means the system is similar in function to Pix — fast, interoperable, account-to-account — but very different in governance.

The main debate revolves around interoperability, access rules, and who gets to participate. Banks appear willing to lead the first phase, but there is pressure to ensure the final model includes fintechs, non-bank issuers, and digital wallets. The central bank is creating the regulatory frame, while the private sector is arguing over how open the network should be. This is not simply a Chilean Pix clone: the central bank’s decision to stay out of the build has created a more complex negotiation among stakeholders.

Regulatory Timeline & What Happens Next

The most concrete official signal came on August 5, 2026, when the Banco Central, presenting its annual payment-systems report, announced it would put a regulatory proposal for an instant payment system out for public consultation. This consultation is the formal step toward setting the rules for the system, but it is far from the final stage. Industry reporting suggests the banking project is not close to launch, with no chance it appears in the next few months because banks still need to agree on technical details and must wait for the central bank’s regulatory process to conclude.

One local report has claimed the central bank is preparing a system to arrive before the end of 2026, but that article is less specific on official milestones and appears more assertive than other sources. Based on the stronger reporting, the safest reading is: consultation in August 2026, implementation still pending, and timing genuinely uncertain. The regulatory process will likely take months, and the private-sector negotiations over access and interoperability could stretch further.

Why Instant Payments in Chile Matter

For merchants and consumers in Chile, instant payments in Chile would mean faster settlement, lower reliance on cards, and potentially lower costs. But the governance model matters as much as the technology. If banks control the network, they may set fees and access conditions that favour incumbents. If fintechs and wallets are included from the start, the system could be more competitive and innovative.

The central bank’s decision to regulate rather than build is a deliberate choice, but it carries risk. Brazil’s Pix succeeded partly because the central bank could impose rules and push adoption. In Chile, the private sector must agree on the details, and that has proven difficult before. For now, the consultation is the only hard date on the calendar, and the industry is watching to see whether Tiro becomes a real system or another failed attempt.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is ‘Tiro’? ‘Tiro’ is the internal name for a private-bank-led project to build a real-time account-to-account payment system in Chile. It would use aliases and QR codes for transfers between people and merchants, and is designed to work on the existing TEF network. How is this different from Brazil’s Pix? Pix was built and operated by Brazil’s central bank. In Chile, the central bank has declined to build the rail itself, leaving the project to private banks and BancoEstado. The central bank is instead creating the regulatory framework for the system. When will the system launch? There is no confirmed launch date. The central bank announced on August 5, 2026 that it will open a public consultation, expected in the third quarter, but industry reports say the project is not expected to launch soon. Timing remains uncertain.

Sources: Chócale; Diario Financiero; BioBioChile; FinteChile; Banco Central de Chile.

World.title: Guyana’s Kurupung Uranium Plan Runs Into Indigenous Opposition
World.content:
Guyana · Mining

Key Facts Project Kurupung Uranium Project, a 92.2 sq km exploration property in Region Seven (Cuyuni-Mazaruni).

Kurupung Uranium Project, a 92.2 sq km exploration property in Region Seven (Cuyuni-Mazaruni). Resource Historical estimate of 20.6 million pounds of uranium; figure is unverified and not current.

Historical estimate of 20.6 million pounds of uranium; figure is unverified and not current. Operator Canada’s U92 Energy Corp, which controls the project via LIA Industries and local subsidiary LIA (Guyana) Inc.

Canada’s U92 Energy Corp, which controls the project via LIA Industries and local subsidiary LIA (Guyana) Inc. Licences Two prospecting licences issued by the GGMC on 19 April 2024, valid for three years with possible extensions.

Two prospecting licences issued by the GGMC on 19 April 2024, valid for three years with possible extensions. Timeline U92 expects phase-one drilling to begin in August 2026, pending EPA approval of its environmental management plan.

U92 expects phase-one drilling to begin in August 2026, pending EPA approval of its environmental management plan. Opposition Amerindian Peoples Association and Region Seven Vice-Chair Alden Marslowe demand a halt over lack of consultation.

A Canadian-controlled uranium exploration project in Guyana’s remote interior is facing mounting Indigenous opposition over consultation gaps, even as regulators weigh approval.

For readers following Latin America’s resource frontier, the Kurupung uranium project in Guyana’s Region Seven has become a flashpoint over how mining licences are issued and who gets a say before drilling begins. The project, controlled by Canada’s U92 Energy Corp, holds a historical resource estimate of 20.6 million pounds of uranium across a 92.2 sq km property. But the controversy is less about the mineral itself than about process: licences were issued in April 2024, yet the public only learned of the project through press reporting in April 2026, and affected communities say they were never properly consulted.

Guyana’s Essequibo river basin, including the Cuyuni-Mazaruni. (Image: Kmusser, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

What is the Kurupung uranium project?

The Kurupung uranium project is an early-stage exploration property in the Cuyuni-Mazaruni region, a heavily forested area in western Guyana. U92 Energy Corp, a Toronto-based company, acquired control earlier in 2026 through the purchase of LIA Industries Pte. Ltd. and its Guyana subsidiary, LIA (Guyana) Inc., which holds the prospecting rights. The local subsidiary was incorporated in Guyana on 20 March 2023, and the Guyana Geology and Mines Commission (GGMC) issued two prospecting licences on 19 April 2024 covering uranium, other radioactive minerals, and rare earth elements.

The licences are valid for three years with possible extensions. U92 has described the project as a priority asset, and has said it expects phase-one drilling to begin in August 2026, once the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) approves its environmental management plan. The historical resource estimate of 20.6 million pounds of uranium dates from earlier work and has not been confirmed under current reporting standards, so it should be treated as an indicative figure rather than a proven reserve.

Who is opposing the project and why?

The most vocal opposition has come from the Amerindian Peoples Association (APA), which has called for the project to be halted. The APA says there has been a lack of public and community-level consultations, and that affected communities were not given enough information before the project advanced. The association has framed the issue as one of consent and information access, arguing that Indigenous peoples in the Middle Mazaruni area have a right to know what is being proposed on their traditional lands before any ground is broken.

Region Seven Vice-Chair Alden Marslowe has also urged the government and the EPA to halt further approvals. In public statements, Marslowe has posted “hands off the Kurupung” and warned that Guyana must not gamble with the future of the Middle Mazaruni. The timing of public awareness is a central grievance: the licences were issued in April 2024, but the project only became widely known through press reporting in April 2026. That two-year gap has fuelled suspicions that decisions were made without adequate transparency.

What is the government’s procedural stance?

The government’s position appears to be one of procedural review rather than outright rejection. The EPA has been reviewing U92’s environmental documents, and the company has said it will not begin drilling until the EPA approves its environmental management plan. That approval process is still pending, and no date for a decision has been publicly confirmed. The government has not signalled any intention to revoke the licences or to impose a moratorium on uranium exploration.

Separately, reporting indicates that the Guyana government has not yet fixed a royalty rate for any future uranium production at Kurupung. Company filings state that the rate would be negotiated when a mining-permit application is made, meaning the fiscal terms for any eventual mine remain undefined. This procedural approach — allowing exploration to proceed while deferring key decisions on royalties and final approvals — has done little to assuage critics who argue that consultation should happen before licences are granted, not after.

What happens next?

The immediate test is the EPA’s review of U92’s environmental management plan. If approved, the company has said it will begin phase-one drilling in August 2026. That timeline could slip, however, given the political and legal pressure building around the project. The APA and regional leaders have not indicated they will accept an EPA approval without further challenge, and the absence of a fixed royalty rate leaves a significant unresolved issue for any future development.

For the Guyana government, the Kurupung uranium project presents a delicate balancing act. On one hand, the country is seeking to diversify its mining sector beyond gold and bauxite, and uranium could be a strategic export. On the other, the government has repeatedly committed to free, prior and informed consent for Indigenous communities under international frameworks. The gap between those commitments and the actual sequence of events at Kurupung — licences first, consultation later — is now the central point of contention.

Frequently Asked Questions

Where is the Kurupung uranium project located? The project is in Region Seven (Cuyuni-Mazaruni) in western Guyana, a remote area with significant Indigenous communities. The property covers roughly 92.2 square kilometres. Who owns the project? Canada’s U92 Energy Corp controls the project through its acquisition of LIA Industries Pte. Ltd. and the Guyana subsidiary LIA (Guyana) Inc., which holds the prospecting licences. Why are Indigenous groups opposed? The Amerindian Peoples Association and regional leaders say affected communities were not properly consulted and were not given enough information before the project advanced. The licences were issued in April 2024, but the public only learned of the project in April 2026.

Sources: Kaieteur News; Amerindian Peoples Association; U92 Energy Corp filings; Guyana EPA.

World.title: Suriname Moves to Evict Mennonite Settlers From Its Rainforest Interior
World.content:
Suriname · Environment

Key Facts Action President Jennifer Geerlings-Simons announced a crackdown on 4 August 2026 against Mennonite-linked settlers and other illegal land occupiers in Suriname’s interior.

President Jennifer Geerlings-Simons announced a crackdown on 4 August 2026 against Mennonite-linked settlers and other illegal land occupiers in Suriname’s interior. Notices Bailiff-delivered eviction notices (deurwaardersexploten) have been issued; illegal residents face deportation.

Bailiff-delivered eviction notices (deurwaardersexploten) have been issued; illegal residents face deportation. Scale The government is reversing prior land allocations covering several hundred thousand hectares, including a reported plan involving 467,000 hectares of mostly primary forest.

The government is reversing prior land allocations covering several hundred thousand hectares, including a reported plan involving 467,000 hectares of mostly primary forest. Task force A special team including police, attorneys, and forest rangers has been created to investigate unauthorised occupation and clearing.

A special team including police, attorneys, and forest rangers has been created to investigate unauthorised occupation and clearing. Policy Agriculture is permitted in the coastal plain but not in the interior rainforest, according to the administration.

Agriculture is permitted in the coastal plain but not in the interior rainforest, according to the administration. Context The move follows years of controversy over Mennonite-linked agricultural projects and Amazon deforestation concerns.

Suriname’s new president has ordered evictions and a task-force probe into unauthorised forest clearing by Mennonite settlers and others in the interior, reversing large land allocations and drawing a firm line between coastal farming and rainforest protection.

For readers following Latin America’s environmental politics, Suriname has just delivered a striking reversal: President Jennifer Geerlings-Simons, in office only months, announced on 4 August 2026 that her government will not tolerate illegal settlement or deforestation in the country’s vast interior, issuing bailiff eviction notices to Mennonite settlers and other land occupiers and creating a special task force to investigate violations. The move signals a sharp break from previous land policies that had allocated hundreds of thousands of hectares of primary forest for agricultural development.

Rainforest along a river in the interior of Suriname. (Photo: Erwin Neles, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

Eviction notices and a new task force

The immediate action is not a mass expulsion already carried out, but a formal legal and administrative crackdown. According to reporting, some Mennonite settlers and other land developers have received a deurwaardersexploot — a written notice delivered by a bailiff — telling them to leave the area. President Simons has said that people found to be illegally on the land will be deported.

A special team, including government officials, police, attorneys, and forest rangers, has been set up to investigate unauthorised occupation and forest clearing, compile violations, and issue eviction or cease-and-desist orders. John Goedschalk, described as a climate adviser to the president, said the task force would examine the extent of illegal activity and enforce the law.

The scale: hundreds of thousands of hectares at stake

The administration says it is reversing land transfers from the previous government involving “several hundred thousand hectares” that had been moved into agricultural use. One report specifies a prior plan involving 467,000 hectares of mostly primary forest slated for agricultural development. Another says the earlier land inventory found that hundreds of thousands of hectares had been allocated through the Ministry of Agriculture, Livestock and Fisheries and should be returned to the state.

This is not a small dispute over a few farms. The figures point to a sweeping re-evaluation of land governance in a country where the interior is largely rainforest and home to Indigenous and Maroon communities. The previous allocations, now under review, had been connected to Mennonite-linked agricultural projects that drew criticism from conservation groups and Indigenous leaders, some of whom had already mobilised against earlier settlement plans in 2024.

Government’s position: coastal farming, not rainforest clearance

President Simons has been explicit about the policy distinction. Agriculture is acceptable in the coastal plain, she said, but not in the interior rainforest. The government will not allow groups to settle in remote areas, clear forest, and build communities there, while legal farming can proceed in the coastal zone. She also said the administration is evaluating migration policy and tightening enforcement against illegal settlement and deforestation.

The position is a direct rebuke to previous arrangements that had allowed or encouraged agricultural development inland. By framing the issue as one of legality and environmental protection, the government is attempting to reset the terms of land use in Suriname — and to signal to foreign agricultural investors that the interior is not open for business.

Amazon-protection context and earlier project history

The crackdown sits within a wider regional debate over Amazon rainforest protection, land governance, and rural development. Suriname, though small in population, holds a significant share of the Guiana Shield forest, one of the world’s most intact tropical forest blocks. The reported land allocations — and the clearing associated with them — had become a flashpoint for conservation concerns.

Earlier project iterations help explain the sensitivity. An earlier Terra Invest plan that surfaced in 2023 aimed to secure about 30,000 hectares for roughly 1,000 Mennonite families — a figure environmental groups feared could balloon toward 90,000 hectares. A pilot for about 50 families was cancelled in March 2024 amid conservation and Indigenous objections. Those figures predate the 2026 eviction action, but they show the scale of ambition that preceded the current reversal. The government’s new stance, with its task force and eviction notices, is an attempt to draw a clear line between legal coastal agriculture and illegal rainforest settlement.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Suriname expelling all Mennonites? No. The government is targeting illegal settlement and land clearing connected to Mennonite-linked groups and other occupiers, not the Mennonite community as a whole. Legal agricultural activity in the coastal plain remains permitted. How much land is affected by the reversal? Reports refer to several hundred thousand hectares of prior allocations, with one figure citing 467,000 hectares of mostly primary forest. The exact total under review has not been fully confirmed. What happens to people who received eviction notices? Those found to be illegally on the land face deportation, according to President Simons. A task force is compiling violations and issuing eviction or cease-and-desist orders, with enforcement involving police and forest rangers.

Sources: Mongabay; Suriname Times; office of the President of Suriname.

World.title: Peru’s Government Rules Out Pardons for Toledo and Castillo
World.content:
Peru · Politics

Key Facts Aug 3, 2026 President Keiko Fujimori said Alejandro Toledo’s humanitarian pardon request would be evaluated on technical, medical and humanitarian grounds.

President Keiko Fujimori said Alejandro Toledo’s humanitarian pardon request would be evaluated on technical, medical and humanitarian grounds. Aug 8, 2026 Justice Minister Ernesto Álvarez ruled out an immediate pardon for Toledo, saying “No se puede indultar a Toledo”.

Justice Minister Ernesto Álvarez ruled out an immediate pardon for Toledo, saying “No se puede indultar a Toledo”. Same day Álvarez called a pardon for Pedro Castillo “impossible” in the current scenario.

Álvarez called a pardon for Pedro Castillo “impossible” in the current scenario. Toledo is serving two corruption sentences at Barbadillo prison linked to the Odebrecht scandal, including a 13-year-4-month term added in 2025.

is serving two corruption sentences at Barbadillo prison linked to the Odebrecht scandal, including a 13-year-4-month term added in 2025. Castillo is serving 11 years 5 months for his failed 2022 self-coup attempt.

is serving 11 years 5 months for his failed 2022 self-coup attempt. No pardon has been granted to either former president as of mid-August 2026.

Peru’s government has sent mixed signals on clemency for two jailed former presidents, ultimately slamming the door on both.

For anyone following Latin America’s judicial and political turbulence, the cases of Toledo and Castillo in Peru are a reminder that presidential pardons are rarely simple legal acts — they are political minefields. In the space of five days in August 2026, President Keiko Fujimori’s administration first suggested a humanitarian pardon for ex-president Alejandro Toledo was under review, then flatly ruled it out, while also declaring a pardon for Pedro Castillo “impossible”. The statements clarify little about the men’s fates, but they reveal much about the political calculations of a government navigating corruption convictions, coup attempts and public anger.

The Palace of Justice in Lima, Peru. (Photo: Art DiNo, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

A Pardon That Wasn’t

On 3 August 2026, President Fujimori told reporters that Toledo’s humanitarian pardon request “is going to be evaluated with two types of analysis: a technical and medical character, and also with a humanitarian view”. She added that the Commission on Pardons and Presidential Graces first needed to be formed before any analysis could begin. The statement appeared to open a window for the 80-year-old former president, who has cancer and has been held at the Barbadillo prison since his extradition from the United States.

Five days later, Justice Minister Ernesto Álvarez slammed that window shut. In an interview with Panamericana TV, he said the government did not currently contemplate granting a pardon to Toledo. “One cannot pardon Toledo,” he said, explaining that presidential graces depend essentially on “a state of serious illness”. Álvarez stressed that any evaluation could only proceed if medical reports corroborate the severity of Toledo’s cancer. The shift in tone was abrupt, suggesting either internal disagreement or a deliberate two-step approach to test public reaction.

Castillo: A Political and Legal Dead End

Álvarez was also asked about Pedro Castillo, the former rural schoolteacher turned president who attempted to dissolve Congress in December 2022. His answer was categorical: “In this scenario it is impossible. Legally, the Peruvian state already has a legal solution and this is already public.” The minister went further, describing protests calling for Castillo’s release as “blackmail” and insisting he would not be swayed unless Castillo faced a serious illness or grave problem.

Castillo is serving an 11-year-5-month sentence for his failed self-coup, a term that many legal analysts considered relatively lenient given the severity of the charge. But for the Fujimori government, any move toward clemency would be politically toxic. Castillo retains a loyal base in Peru’s southern highlands, and his supporters have repeatedly taken to the streets. Granting him a pardon would be read as capitulation to that pressure — something Álvarez explicitly rejected by using the word “blackmail”.

The Legal Status of Toledo and Castillo

Toledo and Castillo occupy different legal universes, though they share the same prison complex. Toledo, Peru’s president from 2001 to 2006, has been convicted twice in connection with the Odebrecht corruption scandal. Reports cite sentences of more than 30 years in total, with RPP noting that in 2025 he received an additional 13 years and 4 months for aggravated money laundering. His humanitarian pardon request rests on his cancer diagnosis, but the government has made clear that medical evidence must be unambiguous before any mercy is shown.

Castillo’s case is more straightforward in legal terms: he was tried and convicted for a specific act — attempting to shut down Congress and rule by decree. There is no corruption angle, no foreign bribery scandal, no complex financial web. It was a direct challenge to Peru’s constitutional order, and the judiciary responded with a firm sentence. For the government, pardoning Castillo would not only be politically dangerous but would also undermine the institutional response to the 2022 crisis.

Politics, Pardons and Perception

The Fujimori administration’s handling of both cases reflects a broader tension in Peruvian politics. Keiko Fujimori herself spent 16 months in pre-trial detention between 2018 and 2020 on corruption charges, and she knows better than most how the public reads acts of executive clemency. Her father, Alberto Fujimori, was pardoned in 2017 by then-president Pedro Pablo Kuczynski — a decision that triggered massive protests and was later annulled by the courts. The political cost of that pardon still echoes in Lima’s corridors of power.

By first suggesting Toledo’s case would be reviewed, then rejecting it, the government may have been testing the waters. But the final message is clear: no pardons for Toledo and Castillo in the current scenario. For Toledo, the door remains theoretically open if his health deteriorates further and medical reports confirm it. For Castillo, the door appears welded shut. The contrast is telling — one former president may yet benefit from humanitarian considerations, while the other is treated as a constitutional threat with no path to clemency. In Peru’s deeply polarised climate, that distinction is unlikely to satisfy anyone.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did the government first say Toledo’s pardon would be evaluated, then rule it out? President Fujimori initially said the request would be assessed on technical, medical and humanitarian grounds. Five days later, Justice Minister Ernesto Álvarez said the government did not currently contemplate a pardon, citing the requirement of a serious illness corroborated by medical reports. The reversal may reflect internal debate or a cautious approach to public opinion. Can Pedro Castillo be pardoned under Peruvian law? Technically, a presidential pardon is possible for any convicted person. However, the Justice Minister has said it is “impossible” in the current scenario, and the government views protests for Castillo’s release as “blackmail”. A pardon would require a major political shift. What is Alejandro Toledo’s current legal situation? Toledo is imprisoned at Barbadillo prison serving two corruption sentences linked to the Odebrecht scandal. In 2025, he received an additional sentence of 13 years and 4 months for aggravated money laundering. His humanitarian pardon request remains under political and technical evaluation, but has not been granted.

Sources: La República; Infobae; Diario Correo; RPP; Panamericana TV.

World.title: Argentina’s UVA Mortgages Are Back, but the Recovery Is Fragile
World.content:
Argentina · Economy

Key Facts June 2026 originations About 1,850 UVA mortgages worth roughly US$150 million, the best monthly figure since March but nearly 50% below a year earlier.

About 1,850 UVA mortgages worth roughly US$150 million, the best monthly figure since March but nearly 50% below a year earlier. Early-2026 slump In the first four months of 2026, mortgage originations fell about 30% year on year (8,717 loans versus 12,191).

In the first four months of 2026, mortgage originations fell about 30% year on year (8,717 loans versus 12,191). Rate range Banco Municipal de Rosario offered about 4.2% TNA plus UVA; Banco Nacion about 6.0% for salary-account clients; other lenders ran from roughly 9.5% to 10.5%.

Banco Municipal de Rosario offered about 4.2% TNA plus UVA; Banco Nacion about 6.0% for salary-account clients; other lenders ran from roughly 9.5% to 10.5%. Affordability cap Banks generally cap the initial installment at about 25% of household income when originating a loan.

Banks generally cap the initial installment at about 25% of household income when originating a loan. Court cap A federal appeals court in Resistencia in 2026 confirmed a 30%-of-salary limit on UVA installments under the “shared effort” doctrine.

A federal appeals court in Resistencia in 2026 confirmed a 30%-of-salary limit on UVA installments under the “shared effort” doctrine. Funding bottleneck Banks lend short-term deposits against 20–30 year mortgages; the government has discussed using the ANSeS FGS fund for long-term financing.

Argentina’s inflation-indexed UVA mortgages have made a modest comeback under Milei, but affordability fears and a funding mismatch keep the market fragile.

For anyone tracking Latin America’s most watched economy, Argentina’s UVA mortgages are a useful barometer: they returned with much fanfare in 2024 as inflation cooled, yet the latest data show a recovery that is real but shallow, and still hostage to the same indexation risk that burned borrowers during the 2018–2019 crisis.

A residential neighbourhood in Buenos Aires. (Photo: Alex O’Neal, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

A revival from a low base

The numbers tell a story of stabilisation rather than boom. In June 2026, banks granted about 1,850 UVA mortgages worth roughly US$150 million — the best monthly figure since March 2026, but still about 50% below the same month a year earlier. The early part of the year was weaker: in the first four months of 2026, originations fell roughly 30% year on year, with about 8,717 loans versus 12,191 in the same period of 2025. The city of Buenos Aires, the traditional heart of the mortgage market, was down about 31.6%.

That performance reflects a recovery from a very low base. UVA mortgages were effectively frozen for years after the 2018 currency crisis, and their return under President Javier Milei was hailed as a sign of financial normalisation. Banks across the system now offer them, including Banco Nacion, Banco Ciudad, BBVA, ICBC, Banco Macro, Santander and Banco Hipotecario. Rates vary widely: Banco Municipal de Rosario offers the lowest at about 4.2% TNA plus UVA, while Banco Nacion charges about 6.0% for salary-account clients; other lenders run from roughly 9.5% to 10.5%.

The indexation risk that never went away

The core concern with UVA mortgages is structural: the loan balance and the monthly installment rise with inflation, while the starting interest rate is fixed. That means borrowers’ payments are tied to the UVA index, not to their wages. If salaries lag inflation — as they have done in several recent episodes — the installment can consume a growing share of income, making the loan progressively harder to service.

To contain that risk at origination, banks generally cap the initial installment at about 25% of household income. This is a prudent underwriting rule, but it does not protect against future divergence between inflation and wage growth. The problem is not hypothetical: during the 2018–2019 crisis, many UVA borrowers saw their installments jump far faster than their pay, prompting a wave of court cases and political pressure.

The 25% and 30% caps

Two distinct caps are often conflated, and it is worth keeping them separate. The first is the bank-level underwriting rule of roughly 25% of household income for the initial installment. This is a private-sector standard, applied when the loan is originated, and it varies slightly by bank and borrower profile.

The second is a court-imposed limit. Invoking the “esfuerzo compartido” (shared-effort) doctrine, some courts have capped UVA installments at 30% of the borrower’s salary. In 2026, a federal appeals court in Resistencia confirmed such a 30%-of-salary limit. This judicial intervention adds legal uncertainty for lenders, as it effectively rewrites the contract terms after origination, and it creates a patchwork of rulings across the country.

Funding remains the bottleneck

Beyond affordability, the market faces a deeper structural problem: funding. Banks lend short-term deposits against 20–30 year mortgages, a classic maturity mismatch. In a country with volatile deposits and high inflation history, this mismatch is especially acute. Banks are reluctant to commit long-term capital at fixed spreads when their funding base can evaporate quickly.

The government has floated the idea of using the ANSeS Fondo de Garantia de Sustentabilidad (FGS), the state pension fund, to provide long-term funding. That would address the maturity mismatch, but it also raises questions about the use of public pension assets for housing policy. For now, the market remains dependent on bank balance sheets, which explains why volumes are still far below the levels seen before the 2018 crisis. The revival under Milei is genuine, but it is a fragile one — and it will stay that way until the funding question is resolved.

Frequently Asked Questions

How do UVA mortgages work? UVA mortgages are indexed to inflation via the UVA unit. The loan balance and the monthly installment rise with inflation, while the starting interest rate is fixed. This means payments can increase over time even if the borrower’s salary does not. What is the difference between the 25% and 30% caps? The 25% cap is a bank underwriting rule applied at origination, limiting the initial installment to about a quarter of household income. The 30% cap is a court-imposed limit on installments as a share of salary, applied in some cases under the “shared effort” doctrine. They are separate mechanisms. Why is funding a problem for UVA mortgages? Banks fund 20–30 year mortgages with short-term deposits, creating a maturity mismatch. If deposits leave or rates rise, banks may not be able to sustain long-term lending. The government has discussed using the ANSeS FGS fund to provide longer-term financing, but no final decision has been confirmed.

Sources: La Nación; Ámbito; Infobae; El Cronista; Perfil.

World.title: Colombia’s Infrastructure Chamber Warns of Stalled Projects, Not Money
World.content:
Colombia · Infrastructure

Key Facts Airport projects 14 regional airport projects are planned in Colombia.

14 regional airport projects are planned in Colombia. Active contracts Only 6 of those 14 projects have live contracts in place.

Only 6 of those 14 projects have live contracts in place. Physical progress Progress on the active airport projects is under 3%.

Progress on the active airport projects is under 3%. Core bottleneck Slow coordination between ANI and Aerocivil is cited as the main problem.

Slow coordination between ANI and Aerocivil is cited as the main problem. CCI warning The chamber says project paralysis and contract delays, not lack of money, are the key risks.

The chamber says project paralysis and contract delays, not lack of money, are the key risks. Priority works CCI urges fast-tracking four major airport initiatives, including Bogotá El Dorado and Cali.

Colombia’s infrastructure chamber warns that institutional delays, not financing gaps, are stalling key airport and transport projects under the new government.

For anyone tracking Latin America’s fourth-largest economy, the warning from Colombia’s infrastructure chamber (CCI) is a sobering signal: the country’s ambitious project pipeline is not failing for lack of money, but for lack of momentum. In a detailed assessment presented to the incoming administration, the CCI said that only 6 of 14 planned regional airport projects have active contracts, and that physical progress on those works is under 3%. The core problem, according to the chamber, is slow coordination between the national infrastructure agency ANI and the civil aviation authority Aerocivil. That means Colombia infrastructure, a sector the government has touted as a growth driver, is at risk of becoming a bottleneck itself.

Construction on Colombia’s Ruta del Sol highway. (Photo: Aguilacansada, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

A warning about paralysis, not funding

The CCI’s message is deliberately framed to counter the assumption that budget constraints are the main obstacle. Instead, the chamber points to project paralysis, contract delays, and institutional bottlenecks as the primary drags on execution under the new government. In the airport segment, the figures are stark: of the 14 regional projects planned, only six have contracts that are actually live, and even those are barely moving, with physical progress below 3%.

These regional airports fall under the aviation authority Aerocivil, and the chamber attributes the delays mainly to its deficient planning and inefficient execution, with permitting, approvals and technical clearances stuck. The airport figures come from the CCI’s quarterly “Infra A Fondo” tracking; the warning is not isolated, and it accompanies a broader “hoja de ruta” (roadmap) that the CCI, led by executive president María Consuelo Araújo Castro, presented on 16 July 2026, urging the new administration to treat infrastructure as a state policy, with legal certainty and regulatory stability across road, rail, airport, port, and river projects.

The airport numbers that matter

The most concrete figures in the CCI’s report concern regional airports. The 14 planned projects are meant to improve connectivity in secondary cities and rural areas, but the current status suggests that many will not deliver on schedule. With only six contracts active and progress under 3%, the risk is that even those projects with signed agreements may stall if inter-agency coordination does not improve quickly.

The CCI also urged the government to fast-track four major airport works already backed by private initiatives: Bogotá El Dorado, Cali Alfonso Bonilla Aragón, Cartagena airport, and a new runway in Antioquia. These are not speculative proposals; they are projects with existing private-sector interest and financing structures. The chamber’s point is that these should be prioritised to demonstrate that the system can still deliver.

Institutional delay as the main risk

The CCI’s analysis consistently returns to one theme: the sector’s main risk is institutional delay, not financing scarcity. This is a significant shift in tone from previous years, when budget availability was often the central concern. Now, the chamber is telling the new government that private capital will only move if bureaucratic friction is reduced and legal certainty is guaranteed.

That message has direct implications for investment. If contractors and financiers see that projects can be signed but not advanced, they will price in higher risk or simply wait. The CCI’s broader argument is that Colombia infrastructure needs a predictable regulatory environment, not just more money in the budget. The roadmap presented in July is an attempt to lock in that stability across administrations, treating infrastructure as a long-term state priority rather than a political football.

What is at stake for growth and jobs

The stakes go beyond airports. The CCI has linked its warnings to the wider economic picture, arguing that more infrastructure investment could materially lift growth and employment. In a country where transport costs and logistics inefficiencies are persistent drags on competitiveness, stalled projects have a direct cost in lost output and delayed regional development.

For the new government, the choice is clear in the chamber’s framing: reduce institutional bottlenecks and fast-track private initiatives, or accept that the project pipeline will continue to underperform. The CCI’s figures on regional airports are a warning, but they are also a test. If the administration can show progress on the four priority airport works and improve Aerocivil’s planning and execution, it will signal that the paralysis is reversible. If not, the under-3% progress rate may become the norm for the entire infrastructure sector.

Frequently Asked Questions

What exactly did the CCI warn about? The CCI warned that project paralysis, contract delays, and institutional bottlenecks are slowing infrastructure execution under the new government. It specifically noted that only 6 of 14 regional airport projects have active contracts and physical progress is under 3%. Why is the airport progress rate so low? The chamber attributes the low progress mainly to Aerocivil’s weak planning and execution. Strikingly, about half the assigned money is already committed while physical progress sits near 2%, so even funded projects are barely advancing on the ground. What does the CCI want the government to do? The CCI presented a roadmap on 16 July 2026 urging the administration to treat infrastructure as a state policy, ensure legal certainty, and fast-track four major airport works already backed by private initiatives, including Bogotá El Dorado and Cali.

Sources: Cámara Colombiana de la Infraestructura; El Tiempo; Portafolio; La República; Valora Analítik.

World.title: Nearly 3 Million Mexican Jobs Are Exposed to Generative AI
World.content:
Mexico · Economy

Key Facts Affected jobs An estimated 2.93 million Mexican jobs, or 4.9% of the labour market, sit in occupations with medium-to-high exposure to generative AI.

An estimated 2.93 million Mexican jobs, or 4.9% of the labour market, sit in occupations with medium-to-high exposure to generative AI. Not automatic loss The analysis breaks jobs into tasks and assesses which could be performed or facilitated by current AI, explicitly noting this does not mean the job will disappear.

The analysis breaks jobs into tasks and assesses which could be performed or facilitated by current AI, explicitly noting this does not mean the job will disappear. Gender gap Roughly 1.87 million women (7.7% of female workers) are in medium-to-high-exposure roles, versus 1.06 million men (about 3% of male workers).

Roughly 1.87 million women (7.7% of female workers) are in medium-to-high-exposure roles, versus 1.06 million men (about 3% of male workers). Source The estimate comes from the observatory México, ¿cómo vamos?, with senior analyst Juvenal Campos among the specialists presenting it.

The estimate comes from the observatory México, ¿cómo vamos?, with senior analyst Juvenal Campos among the specialists presenting it. BMV plan The Mexican Stock Exchange (BMV) and its rival BIVA have publicly discussed whether the market could handle 24-hour trading, though there is no firm plan or timeline.

The Mexican Stock Exchange (BMV) and its rival BIVA have publicly discussed whether the market could handle 24-hour trading, though there is no firm plan or timeline. Separate tracks The AI-exposure study and the BMV trading-hours plan are distinct developments, not directly linked in the supplied material.

A new analysis quantifies which Mexican workers face the highest task-level exposure to generative AI, while the stock exchange weighs longer trading hours.

For anyone following Latin America’s largest economy, the twin signals from Mexico this week are worth separating: one is a sober, task-based estimate of how generative AI might reshape the labour force, and the other is a market-structure shift at the Mexican Stock Exchange (BMV) toward 24-hour trading. Neither implies an imminent upheaval, but together they point to a country bracing for faster technological and financial change.

The Mexican Stock Exchange (BMV) in Mexico City. (Photo: Bohao Zhao, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

One-stop reference Company Intelligence Every listed company in Latin America — financials, ownership and structure for 1,450+ companies across 26 exchanges, in one place. Browse the directory →

What the AI exposure in Mexico study actually says

The figure of 4.9% of jobs—about 2.93 million positions—comes from an analysis by México, ¿cómo vamos?, a civil-society observatory that tracks economic and social indicators. The study does not predict mass unemployment. Instead, it evaluates each occupation by breaking it into concrete tasks and asking which of those tasks could be performed or facilitated by generative AI with current capabilities. Occupations are then classified by medium or high exposure, meaning a significant share of their routine tasks could be automated or augmented.

The gender breakdown is striking: 1.87 million women are in exposed roles, equivalent to 7.7% of female workers, compared with 1.06 million men, or about 3% of male workers. This suggests that clerical, administrative, and certain professional roles—where women are overrepresented in Mexico’s formal labour market—are more likely to involve tasks that AI can already handle. The authors, including senior analyst Juvenal Campos, stress that exposure is not the same as displacement; many workers could see their tasks reframed rather than eliminated.
