NEW DELHI: Isha Foundation founder Sadhguru on Monday launched a new photography book called "Disappearing Faces", featuring photographs of people he encountered during his journeys through the remote Himalayas of Nepal and Tibet.Published by Penguin India, the book was launched by Union minister Mansukh Mandaviya at the India International Centre in New Delhi.The launch was followed by a conversation between Sadhguru and commentator Anand Ranganathan, exploring the stories and experiences behind the photographs featured in the book.âThese faces represent an era that will soon disappear: faces etched only by sensory perception of light and darkness, heat and cold, of springs and winters - above all, uncontaminated by information that is disconnected from our senses. Our senses lead to a certain sense of life where there is no Non-sense," Sadhguru said during the conversation."These are the visages that represent life that seems rudimentary but is rich with strong experiences of the land, the winds, the waters and the people. Over the last five decades, year after year, beyond the beauty and wondrous nature of the mountains, these faces have drawn me into the deep crevices of the Himalayas," he added.Carrying a camera along the way, Sadhguru began documenting faces shaped by a life lived close to nature and increasingly distant from the cities.The book offers an intimate visual record of the people Sadhguru encountered during his journeys.Sadhguru first journeyed to Manasarovar and Mount Kailash in 2006 and has since returned repeatedly, leading seekers on the Himalayan pilgrimage. After undertaking his first motorcycle journey to Kailash in 2025, Sadhguru is set to return once again this year on a motorcycle, continuing his unique engagement with the sacred landscape of the Himalayas.The Himalayas have remained a significant part of Sadhguruâs life over the years, alongside his efforts towards human wellbeing, raising human consciousness and his commitment to ecological regeneration.

World.title: Old allies, new equation? Why SAD and BJP may join hands for 2027 Punjab assembly elections
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Will the BJP and the

revive their decades-old ties in Punjab for the 2027 assembly elections? Haryana chief minister Nayab Singh Saini, who has been playing a key role in BJPâs Punjab plans, has ruled out any such possibility.

His denial comes amid a strong alliance buzz triggered by a meeting between Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Shiromani Akali Dal (SAD) chief Sukhbir Singh Badal last week - the first such meeting after the two parties snapped ties 6 years ago over the 3 farm bills.

BJPâs Saini has played down alliance rumours. When asked to comment on the meeting, Saini replied in Punjabi, "Nahi, aise koyi gall nahi hai (No, there is no such thing)".

The Haryana chief minister said the Prime Minister is the voice of 140 crore people. "If anyone wants to meet him, his doors are open; anyone can meet. Political parties keep meeting him for various issues."

Saini further added, "Bharatiya Janata Party ka gathbandhan Punjab di janta de naal hai. (BJP's alliance is with the people of Punjab). And I say this with great confidence because I meet people there. In Punjab, the BJP is forming its government."





So, can Sainiâs denial be taken at face value? Or is it just political rhetoric to keep pressure on a regional party which appears desperate for an alliance with the BJP?

SAD's electoral decline

Sukhbir Singh Badal, who has served two terms as deputy chief minister of Punjab and whose father Parkash Singh Badal was a 5-time chief minister, has been struggling to make a political comeback in the state. In the last two assembly elections, his party, SAD, has been pushed to the margins.

The decline began in the 2017 assembly elections, when the SAD won only 15 of the 94 seats it contested, with a vote share of 25.24%. This was a sharp decline compared to its 2012 performance when the SAD had won 56 seats with a vote share of 34.73%. If 2017 was a worry, 2022, after it snapped ties with the BJP and contested alone, was a clear warning: the SAD could win only 3 seats, and its vote share dipped to 18.38%.

This decline was not limited to just assembly elections. In the Lok Sabha elections too, SAD suffered a decline.

In 2019, the SAD polled 27.76% of votes and won 2 seats. Five years later, while the seat reduced to 1, the vote share dipped to 13.48%. In 2014, the SAD tally in Lok Sabha was 4 seats and a 26.37% vote share.

Clearly, for Sukhbir Singh Badal, both the crisis and the test are real. And that perhaps explains his visible desperation for an alliance with the BJP. And while the saffron party may reject alliance rumours, the SAD has sent clear signals of a strategic shift â extending a friendly hand to the BJP.

BJP-SAD alliance lasted nearly two decades before the parties split over the farm laws in 2020

Badal's changed tune on delimitation

In April this year, Badal had criticised the Centreâs move on delimitation of Lok Sabha seats in the garb of the Womenâs Reservation Bill. "Punjab is predominantly a minority character state. We will be the biggest victim of this population-based delimitation. Compared with a nominal increase in seats for Punjab, Haryana will witness a nearly hundred per cent increase and double the number of its seats in the Lok Sabha," Badal had then said in a statement.

Four months later, the SAD chief has literally taken a U-turn on the issue. After his meeting with PM Modi, Badal changed his stand and demanded the immediate implementation of the Womenâs Reservation Bill. He also supported the Union governmentâs proposal to increase Parliament seats in states by 50 per cent.

In a new statement after his meeting with PM Modi, Badal said the party stood for a fair and equitable delimitation exercise that ensured equal increase in representation to all states.

âThis will ensure justice is done to all states,â he said.

'Why so desperate for BJP alliance?'

Badalâs changed stand prompted a dig from Punjab Congress president Amarinder Singh Raja Warring, who asked the Shiromani Akali Dal chief as to why he was so desperate for an electoral alliance with the BJP that he had to make a U-turn on a sensitive matter like delimitation of the assembly and parliamentary constituencies.

âWhat changed within these months that you started seeing merit in the same Bill, you otherwise found against Punjabâs interests?â he asked.

âSukhbir has turned more loyal than the king within no time,â Warring said.

He said when the Akalis had failed to reach an alliance with the BJP ahead of the parliamentary elections, Badal had claimed that he did not want to compromise on the interests of Punjab. âNow that you are desperate for your own survival, you have simply forgotten the interests of Punjab for which you claimed to have taken a stand in 2024,â said Warring.

Chief minister Bhagwant Mann also took potshots at Badal and said, "BJP can make them do whatever they want. SAD just wants to get back into the cabinet in Delhi or get into an alliance with the BJP in Punjab."

These reactions would suggest that both the ruling AAP and the Congress are perhaps aware how a potential BJP-Akali alliance could change the dynamics on ground. While they may play down the possible impact of this alliance, they would be keeping a close eye on the developments.

AAP would hope that the 2027 Punjab contest stays four-cornered so that the ruling party can benefit from the division of opposition votes.

The Congress, on the other hand, realises that SAD could help the BJP in rural areas and add to the party's challenges in the state.

Little wonder, Badal would not mind their political barbs as long as he can secure the future of his party with the BJP. And that brings us to Sainiâs remark playing down the meeting between PM Modi and Sukhbir Badal.

Why SAD alliance can help BJP

For the BJP, the Akali association is electorally important, at least for now. The BJP has just two seats in the current assembly with a vote share of 6.6%. The party could not win a single seat in the 2024 Lok Sabha elections despite polling 18.65% of votes. This was almost double of the 9.74% that the BJP managed in 2019 Lok Sabha elections. It was also a huge jump from the 2022 assembly elections when the BJP got just 6.6% of votes.

But the fact that BJP could win 2 Lok Sabha seats in 2019 despite a low vote share points to the importance of SAD alliance in converting votes to seats in the state.

Despite the sharp decline in its electoral fortunes, the Shiromani Akali Dal still has good support base in rural Punjab and also has a strong Sikh-centric regional identity - both of which can help the BJP in case of an alliance. Combined with BJP's urban support base, this can turn into a winning combination for the two parties.

The SAD has been going all out to increase its base and presence in the state.

The controversy around movie Satluj, which narrates the life story of activist Jaswant Singh Khalra - who uncovered alleged extrajudicial cremations in Punjab between mid-1980s and early-1990s, gave SAD the much-needed boost to woo its core voters. When the movie was taken down from the OTT platform, SAD arranged its screening across Punjab.

In a post on X in Punjabi, Badal had then said, "In every village and corner of Punjab, the SAD will screen the film 'Satluj' based on inhuman atrocities inflicted on thousands of innocent Sikh youth and Sikh personalities like Shaheed Bhai Jaswant Singh Ji Khalra during the Congress regime, so that our children and future generations can be thoroughly acquainted with the oppression inflicted.

"

Badal had justified the move and said:"This is aimed at ensuring that today's youth and our coming generations know about the unspeakable tragedy and repression unleashed by the then Congress governments against Bhai Jaswant Singh Khalra and thousands of other innocent Sikh youth who were eliminated through fake encounters."

The aggressive SAD campaign was clearly a move to consolidate its âPanthicâ vote bank - a political mobilisation surrounding the Sikh communityâs collective identity.

The SAD perhaps can complement the BJP if the two parties eventually agree for an alliance.

Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

BJP's bid to dominate?

Hence, the BJPâs posturing vis-a-vis the SAD alliance at present perhaps has more to do with asserting who will dictate terms if and when the two parties join hands. And this is important as till 2020, when the partnership snapped, the SAD was the senior partner in Punjabâs NDA alliance and the BJP played second fiddle. That political dynamic has changed now. By repeatedly asserting that it will contest the

on its own, the BJP has clearly spread the message that it will lead the fight and not play the junior partner to anyone.

Hence, the saffron party would not want to miss any opportunity to reinforce this message to the SAD leadership and its cadres.

True, the BJP is working on a roadmap to increase its political base and strength and become an independent political force in Punjab. This is manifested in the several steps that the party has taken in Punjab. From Prime Ministerâs Punjab rallies to party chief Nitin Nabinâs push and targeted acquisition from political rivals, the BJP has made it clear that it means business in Punjab. But the party perhaps will need more time to do a Bengal in Punjab, if at all it ever happens.

For now, SAD perhaps could be its best bet in Punjab.

NEW DELHI: Pune Police on Tuesday registered an FIR against an Overseas Citizen of India (OCI) cardholder from the United Kingdom for allegedly attempting to convert people to Christianity through religious gatherings.DCP Prashant Amrutkar of the Pune City Police's Special Branch said the accused, a Manchester resident, has been booked under relevant provisions of the Immigration and Foreigners Act, 2025, and the newly enacted Maharashtra Freedom of Religion Act, 2026.According to police, OCI cardholders are permitted to attend prayer meetings and participate in religious functions, but cannot preach or deliver religious speeches without the required permission.Police alleged that the accused spoke about following the path of Jesus and made statements about Hindu temples and deities that they claimed could create misconceptions, news agency ANI reports.The police suspect that the statements were made with the intention of misleading people and inducing them to embrace Christianity. World.title: Centre relaxes construction hurdles in Ganga flood plain
World.content:
The Union government eased restrictions governing construction along the Ganga flood plain this week, paving the way for building projects in areas which are only subject to moderate or rare flooding. This has been done by revising the definition of a ‘flood plain’ and deleting a clause in the legislation that expressly prohibited construction, according to an August 10 gazette order from the National Mission for Clean Ganga (NMCG), affiliated to the Jal Shakti Ministry.

A senior government official told The Hindu that the amendments did not represent any “dilution of standards”, but rather, attempted to correct an inconsistency in the law.

The ₹30,000 crore Namami Ganga mission, part of the NDA government’s ambitious venture to stem pollution in the Ganga river and maintain its ecological health, sources its legal teeth from the River Ganga (Rejuvenation, Protection and Management) Authorities Order, 2016.

‘Construction-free zone’

That notification defines the Ganga ‘flood plain’ as “the area of the river or its tributaries which comes under water on either side of it due to floods corresponding to its greatest flow or with a flood of frequency once-in-a-hundred years.”

The 2016 order included a clause saying: “...the bank of River Ganga and its flood plain shall be a construction free Zone to reduce pollution sources, pressures and to maintain its natural ground water recharge functions…” Other clauses banned construction in the “active flood plain” of the Ganga, though there was no definition of what constituted “active.”

Stratified regulation

However, an amendment to the 2016 order, published on August 10, makes two crucial modifications. It removes the “no construction” clause. It also adopts a stratified definition of ‘flood plain’ based on flood frequency: an ‘active flood plain’, which is immediately along the channel that submerges at least once every five years; a middle ‘regulatory zone’, subject to moderate flooding every five to 25 years; and an outer ‘warning zone’ on the periphery that floods only during severe 25- to 100-year events.

While the new order does not grant blanket permission for development, it replaces the total ban on flood plain construction with a regulated, approval-based system. Strict building prohibitions are now confined exclusively to the ‘active flood plain’, with minor exceptions reserved for temporary setups like religious events.

Beyond that five-year flood line, construction in the ‘regulatory’ and ‘warning’ zones is now permissible, subject to official clearances. However, any project, from roads and bridges to riverfront infrastructure, must still secure prior approval from the NMCG and regional authorities, while adhering to baseline environmental safeguards.

‘No dilution’

A senior government official told The Hindu that the intention behind the amendment was to remove a long-standing inconsistency. The 2016 order had used the term ‘active’ floodplain without defining it. “This wasn’t a problem initially but in the last few years there was feedback from several quarters that this was an inconsistency. The Central Water Commission released guidelines in July 2025 defining active, regulatory and warning zones for floodplains. In India, no State has clearly defined ‘flood plain’ zones. The August amendments now make the notification consistent. There is no dilution of standards at all,” said the official, who did not wish to be named.

In recent months, there have been several petitions before the National Green Tribunal (NGT) against construction along the Ganga and its tributaries, most recently the Gomti in Uttar Pradesh. Litigants have routinely cited the blanket “construction-free zone” mandate in the 2016 order in their petitions against riverfront roads and embankments, as well as in earlier cases involving municipal sewage treatment plants and riverfront works. The Hindu has reached out to the NMCG for clarification.

World.title: Namma Metro records highest daily ridership of August with over 11.19 lakh boardings
World.content:
Namma Metro recorded its highest daily ridership of the month on Monday, August 10, with 11,19,815 passengers boarding, according to data released by Bangalore Metro Rail Corporation Limited (BMRCL) on Tuesday.

The ridership figures were released a day after the Comptroller and Auditor General of India (CAG) flagged concerns over lower-than-projected ridership and performance in the first two phases of the Bengaluru Metro project.

Of the total boardings recorded on Monday, the Purple Line (Line 1) accounted for the highest share with 4,66,371 boardings, followed by the Green Line (Line 2) with 2,85,499. The Yellow Line (Line 3) recorded 92,838 boardings, while 2,75,107 were recorded as interchange passengers. The total stood at 11,19,815 boardings for the day.

The figures come against the backdrop of the CAG’s Performance Audit Report No. 7 of 2026, which examined the implementation of Phase 1 and Phase 2 of the Bengaluru Metro project. The report, tabled in Parliament on Monday, identified shortcomings in planning, land acquisition, project execution, financial management and operations.

The audit noted that the Actual Peak Hour Peak Direction Traffic (PHPDT) recorded on Phase 1 corridors in 2021 was significantly lower than projected. Actual PHPDT ranged between 6,429 and 8,852, compared to projected levels exceeding 15,000.

The CAG also observed that despite the lower-than-expected ridership, BMRCL had not undertaken a study to determine how ridership could be improved or to assess the implications for investments in the heavy metro system.

The audit further questioned the ridership assumptions used to calculate the financial internal rate of return and economic internal rate of return for Phases 1 and 2. It noted that the projected ridership had not been achieved and that BMRCL had not conducted a detailed assessment of the reasons behind the shortfall.
